issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## **Summary**

This RFC proposes to define API to hook into cache systems, allowing downstream projects to trigger recompilation based on externally-defined conditions.


## **Motivation**

Currently, TorchInductor allows various downstream projects/extensions to hook their logic into its existing infrastructure, e.g. register custom FX optimization passes for Inductor or register custom device backends.
This is very helpful when implementing support or optimizations for specific devices.

In the pursuit of providing maximum level of performance, the Inductor relies on its cache mechanism, reusing previously generated artifacts and not triggering re-compilation when it's not necessary.

The framework relies on multiple levels of cache in the TorchInductor compilation path: there is FXGraphCache, AOTCache and DynamoCache, all of which playing its own role in deciding whether to issue a recompilation for the current launch of the model, or to re-use cached artifacts.

This is very robust and mature system, however there is a limitation within the current implementation: the existing cache mechanism does not allow any external conditions to be included in the validity checks, which might affect  correctness and/or performance of the artifacts generated by the downstream projects. In other words: custom backend might need to raise a re-compilation need in some externally defined circumstances, but currently there is no possibility to do that.


## **Solution proposal**

For the purposes of further explanation, let's refer to the code belonging to a downstream project wanting to use this mechanism, as a *'user code'* (note that actual PyTorch's users might also use this mechanism for their purposes), in opposition to the current framework's code.

The proposed solution is to introduce hooks in the existing caching systems and provide users with API, so that they could register their own set of predicates/conditions, evaluated/established based on some context generally available on the corresponding cache system level. The context provided to the users' callback must be reasonable broad, to allow them to construct valid and meaningful invariants.

In order for this solution to work reliably, it must provide means for affecting all mentioned above cache levels - from DynamoCache, through AOTCache, to FXGraphCache.

The AOTCache and FXGraphCache systems work very similar to each other (at least in the scope we care about in this RFC, so in terms of deciding about cache hit/miss), and we can reason about them together, while the DynamoCache is a different system and will need a different approach.

### A) DynamoCache

#### Overview

DynamoCache is driven by the TorchDynamo guards' mechanism. Affecting DynamoCache's hit/miss decision could be done by introducing a small, opt-in extension point in [torch/_dynamo/guards.py](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/torch/_dynamo/guards.py), that allows users to register a callback which produces an additional runtime lambda guard during guards' assembly.

This callback will have access to the context generally available during the TorchDynamo guards' installation - an instance of [GuardBuilder](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/torch/_dynamo/guards.py#L1013), so when called, the user's code could provide necessary data to assemble a Dynamo guard just like it would if the code was included in the framework.

#### Proposed API

The data necessary for assembling such guard, might look like follow:

```python
@dataclass
class CustomGuardSpec:
    """
    Struct describing data of a custom guard.
    """

    # custom closure variables the guard function should capture
    closure_vars: Dict[str, Any]

    # a single Python expression string that returns True/False at guard time;
    # it can access `closure_vars`
    code: str

    # a human-readable, debug-oriented rendering of the guard logic.
    # If not provided, `code` will be used instead.
    verbose_code: Optional[str]

    # optional name for logs
    name: Optional[str] = None
```

Having that defined, we can draft the following callback registration API:
```python
def register_custom_guard(custom_guard_producer_fn: Callable[[GuardBuilderBase], CustomGuardSpec]) -> RemovableHandle:
    # ...
    pass
```

This function will receive a user-provided callable, taking `GuardBuilder` object as an argument, and returning description of the guard to be installed.

This function shall just store user's callable in some registry and return standard [`RemovableHandle`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/torch/utils/hooks.py#L10), so that users can unregister their checks, when they need to.

#### Usage example

In order to demonstrate a usage pattern, let's write a test for the API we've drafted above.

This is a test for artificial scenario, installing custom guard which asserts on the **value** of the input tensor. It's obviously a non-practical example, but it demonstrates the usage and makes sure we're testing this specific custom guard and no built-in guard is interfering.

```python
# file: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/test/dynamo/test_guard_manager.py
# ...standard import for test/dynamo/test_guard_manager.py...

import torch._dynamo
from torch._dynamo.testing import CompileCounter
from torch._dynamo.source import LocalSource

# 0) assume CustomGuardSpec and register_custom_guard are part of the torch._dynamo.guards:
from torch._dynamo.guards import CustomGuardSpec, register_custom_guard

class CustomGuardRegistrationTests(torch._dynamo.test_case.TestCase):

    def test_custom_guard_can_access_builder_and_closure_vars(self):
        """
        Test whether custom guard works properly: can access `builder` and `closure_vars`
        during tracing and during subsequent runs.
        Test scenario is installing silly custom  guard which will be guarding on value
        of the graph argument x[0][0] and will trigger recompilation if it changes.
        """

        # 1) define some simple model to be compiled, note it has one input - `x`
        def fn(x):
            return x + 1

        cnt = CompileCounter()
        compiled_fn = torch.compile(fn, backend=cnt, fullgraph=False)

        # 2) define user callback which will produce custom guard
        def custom_guard_producer(builder):
            # 2.1) capture the (0, 0) element value of the arg from the tracing run
            x_0_0 = builder.get(LocalSource("x"))[0][0]

            # 2.2) guard will be true for the tracing run and for any other subsequent run
            # when the value of L['x'] will match, and false when value changes
            return CustomGuardSpec(
                closure_vars={"x_0_0": x_0_0},
                code="L['x'][0][0] == x_0_0",
                name="custom silly assert on x[0][0]",
            )

        # 3) use the proposed API to register custom guard (and unregister in cleanup stage)
        handle = register_custom_guard(custom_guard_producer)
        self.addCleanup(handle.remove)


        # 4) define inputs with the same shape but different values for test
        x1 = torch.ones((4, 4))
        x2 = torch.zeros((4, 4))


        # 5) verify with counters if this guard works as expected
        # 5.1) 1st run compiles
        expected_compilations = 1
        compiled_fn(x1)
        c1 = cnt.frame_count
        self.assertEqual(c1, expected_compilations)

        # 5.2) 2nd run with the same input shouldn't trigger compile
        expected_compilations += 0
        compiled_fn(x1)
        c2 = cnt.frame_count
        self.assertEqual(c2, expected_compilations)

        # 5.3) run with different values should recompile
        expected_compilations += 1
        compiled_fn(x2)
        c3 = cnt.frame_count
        self.assertEqual(c3, expected_compilations)

        # 5.4) subsequent run with the same values should not recompile
        expected_compilations += 0
        compiled_fn(x2)
        c4 = cnt.frame_count
        self.assertEqual(c4, expected_compilations)

```

#### Hook implementation

The only important thing missing is the actual invocation of the callbacks registered by users and guards' installation.

This has to be done during the phase when the regular guards are installed, so that the user can access `GuardBuilder`, and we on the framework side can take the user-defined description to actually construct and install proper guard.

[This place](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/torch/_dynamo/guards.py#L4355-L4356) in `CheckFunctionManager.compile_check_fn` looks like a sensible place to iterate through all the registered callbacks and process them.

Assume we have some helper function `_get_registered_custom_guards()` that will retrieve from our registry an iterable of all the callbacks,
then installing the user-defined guards could look like that:

```python
class CheckFunctionManager:
    def compile_check_fn(
        # ...
    ) -> None:

        # ...

        # generate custom guards from user-registered specs:
        for custom_guard_producer in _get_registered_custom_guards():
            try:
                # call user-defined code to produce the guard spec:
                custom_guard_spec = None
                custom_guard_spec = custom_guard_producer(builder)
                if not isinstance(custom_guard_spec, CustomGuardSpec):
                    raise TypeError("Registered custom guard producer function should "
                                    "return `CustomGuardSpec`!")

                # append the custom guard's expression as a lambda guard
                verbose_code = custom_guard_spec.verbose_code if custom_guard_spec.verbose_code else custom_guard_spec.code
                builder.add_python_lambda_leaf_guard_to_root(
                    [custom_guard_spec.code],
                    [verbose_code],
                    custom_guard_spec.closure_vars)

                # add this custom guard to logs
                add_code_part(custom_guard_spec.code, guard=None, log_only=True)

            except Exception as e:
                logging.getLogger(__name__).exception(
                    "Failed to add registered custom guard '%s': %s",
                    getattr(custom_guard_spec, "name", "--unknown custom guard--"),
                    str(e))

        # OK, all done generating guards
        # ...

```

These changes should be suficient to allow users' to influence the DynamoCache hit/miss decissions.

#### Opens
There are some questions to be answered yet, for example:

A.1) what shall we do when the callback raises and error? Here I'm just logging it and functionally ignoring the error, but we might have some flag (in the config?) deciding what to do in such case.

A.2) The other question is the type of guard we are installing. For the purpose of implementing a PoC backing this RFC, the lambda leaf guard seems reasonable and works well, but maybe there is some better option?


### B) AOTCache, FXGraphCache

#### Overview

Both AOTCache and FXGraphCache are using a simple hash key to decide about cache hit/miss, moreover both systems are taking - among other data - a [`_CompileFxKwargs`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/torch/_inductor/compile_fx.py#L764) instance to be pickled and hashed to produce proper cache key. For this reason we could treat them both the same way.

In order to influence those cache systems, we can just provide the ability to include additional, user-defined data in the already pickled data producing compilation cache key used by AOTAutograd and TorchInductor. This data shouldn't be some static global config file, but rather provided in similar fashion as the solution for the DynamoCache, as a user-defined callbacks producing extra data based on some context available before performing the actual compilation, so it can vary per compilation without affecting a global context.

For the purposes of this RFC, let's just allow one user callback that will produce the extra data for both cache systems at once.

#### Proposed API

The exact data structure may not be strictly defined, as this time we won't need it to construct specific objects based on it. The only requirements here is that the pickler should be able to handle it, and we must have the ability to stable sort the extra data coming from different producers, to produce stable hash. For this reason, we could assume the extra data format as a simple `Dict[str, Any]`.

To register such callback, we can use API similar to previously introduced:

```python
def register_extra_cache_key_data(extra_cache_key_data_producer_fn: Callable[[nn.Module, AOTConfig, List[Any], List[Any]], Dict[str, Any]]) -> RemovableHandle:
    """
    Register a callback that emits a dict with extra values to include into
    the compilation cache key.
    It will influence both AotAutograd's and Inductor's cache key.

    The callback is invoked during aot_autograd compilation and provides the caller broad
    context via the following params:
      - gm: GraphModule,
      - aot_config: AOTConfig,
      - real_inputs: List[Any],
      - fake_inputs: List[Any].

    It must return:
      - dictionary with extra keys used for generating cache key. Returned dict must be
      composed of deterministic, picklable primitives.
    """
    # ...
    pass
```

This function will receive a user-provided callable. The callable shall take as arguments a broad context, including aot_config object, real and fake inputs, and return the dict with extra data.

The purpose of this function shall just be to store user's callable in some registry and return standard `RemovableHandle`, so that users can unregister their extra data generation.

The registration API is similar to the DynamoCache case, so the usage pattern will be also  similar. The nature of this cache hit/miss decision is simpler, so the actual user's code might be a bit easier to understand.

#### Usage example

To demonstrate usage, let's define a simple test which will use some external data, to trigger [`FXGraphCache`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/torch/_inductor/codecache.py#L1210) miss. The test will look very similar for the AOTCache, just the counters' validation will differ, so let's omit that in this document.

For the demonstation, the external data can even not be related in any way to the context we're getting in the callback, but of course the real user code will use them to define their own conditions.

```python
# file: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/test/inductor/test_codecache.py#
# ...standard imports for test/inductor/test_codecache.py...

# 0) assume register_extra_cache_key_data is part of the torch._functorch.aot_autograd:
from torch._functorch.aot_autograd import register_extra_cache_key_data

class TestFxGraphCache(TestCase):

    @config.patch({"fx_graph_cache": True})
    @config.patch({"fx_graph_remote_cache": False})
    @torch._functorch.config.patch({"enable_autograd_cache": False})
    def test_extra_cache_key_data_affects_fxgraph_cache(self):
        """
        Changing extra_cache_key_data should invalidate the Inductor FxGraphCache key.
        We inject the extra_cache_key_data via the register_extra_cache_key_data() hook
        and use runtime-controlled cache_key_value as our extra data.
        """

        # 1) define some simple model to be compiled
        def fn(x):
            return x.sin() * 2 + 1

        compiled = torch.compile(fn, fullgraph=True)

        # 2) define user callback which will produce custom extra data to be included in the cache keys.
        cache_key_value = "A"
        def extra_key_cache_data_producer(gm, aot_config, real_inputs, fake_inputs):
            # Let's just use the simplest scenario possible - an external string value to be included in the extra data.
            # Real user's code will produce the extra data based on the available context.
            return {"cache_key_tag": cache_key_value}

        # 3) use the proposed API to include our externally defined data in the cache keys calculation (and unregister in cleanup stage)
        handle = register_extra_cache_key_data(extra_key_cache_data_producer)
        self.addCleanup(handle.remove)

        # 4) verify with counters if this mechnism will trigger cache misses when expected
        # 4.1) define some helpers for easier assetions
        def assert_fxgraph_cache_miss():
            self.assertEqual(counters["inductor"]["fxgraph_cache_miss"], 1)
            self.assertEqual(counters["inductor"]["fxgraph_cache_hit"], 0)

        def assert_fxgraph_cache_hit():
            self.assertEqual(counters["inductor"]["fxgraph_cache_miss"], 0)
            self.assertEqual(counters["inductor"]["fxgraph_cache_hit"], 1)

        # 4.2) define one and the same input tensor we will use for all runs
        x = torch.randn(16)

        with fresh_cache():
            # 4.3) first compilation should miss regardless of our extra tag
            counters.clear()
            out1 = compiled(x)
            self.assertEqual(fn(x), out1)
            assert_fxgraph_cache_miss()

            # 4.4) new run with same tag should hit
            self.reset()
            counters.clear()
            out2 = compiled(x)
            self.assertEqual(fn(x), out2)
            assert_fxgraph_cache_hit()

            # 4.5) extra cache key data changed, different tag should trigger miss
            cache_key_value = "B"
            self.reset()
            counters.clear()
            out3 = compiled(x)
            self.assertEqual(fn(x), out3)
            assert_fxgraph_cache_miss()

            # 4.6) going back to previous tag should hit
            cache_key_value = "A"
            self.reset()
            counters.clear()
            out4 = compiled(x)
            self.assertEqual(fn(x), out4)
            assert_fxgraph_cache_hit()

            # 4.7) unregistering the extra data producer, no extra tag should trigger miss
            handle.remove()
            self.reset()
            counters.clear()
            out5 = compiled(x)
            self.assertEqual(fn(x), out5)
            assert_fxgraph_cache_miss()

            # 4.8) changing tag with unregistered producer should NOT trigger miss
            cache_key_value = "C"
            self.reset()
            counters.clear()
            out6 = compiled(x)
            self.assertEqual(fn(x), out6)
            assert_fxgraph_cache_hit()

```

#### Hook implementation

There are some bits of design left to be discussed. Let's talk about the place from which the user-registered callbacks will be called and where to store the data gathered from user's code, to be propagated to cache keys calculations.

To store the extra data, we could extend the [`AOTConfig`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/schemas.py#L1066) with the extra field:

```python
@dataclass
class AOTConfig:
    """
    Configuration for AOTDispatcher
    """
    # ...
    extra_cache_key_data: Optional[OrderedDict[str, Any]] = None
```

Here we're already use the `OrderedDict`, as we should sort all the extra fields from all registered callbacks, to include them always in the same order.

Place from where we shall call the users' callbacks, should offer access to the broad context we can pass to users, so that it would be generally useful in making decission about potential recompilation. Access to the real and fake inputs will be valuable, as well as access to the graph module and aot config object. Those are available at the beginning of AOTAutograd stage1 of compilation.

The proper place seems to be [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/torch/_functorch/aot_autograd.py#L1057), inside the `prepare_aot_module_simplified` function from `torch/_functorch/aot_autograd.py`:

```python
def prepare_aot_module_simplified(
    # ...
) -> tuple[
    # ...
]:
    # ...

    # if any extra cache key data producers are registered, append them to the aot_config
    # to be eventually passed to _CompileFxKwargs for inclusion in cache key generation
    for extra_cache_key_producer in _get_registered_extra_cache_key_data():
        try:
            extra_data_dict = extra_cache_key_producer(mod, aot_config, args, fake_flat_args)
            if aot_config.extra_cache_key_data is None:
                aot_config.extra_cache_key_data = OrderedDict()
            logging.getLogger(__name__).debug("Updating extra_cache_key_data with the follwing keys: %s",
                                              extra_data_dict.keys())
            aot_config.extra_cache_key_data.update(extra_data_dict)

        except Exception:
            logging.getLogger(__name__).exception("Failed to add extra cache key data.")

    # include the extra data always in the same order, regardless of registration order
    if aot_config.extra_cache_key_data is not None:
        extra_data_sorted_by_keys = OrderedDict(sorted(aot_config.extra_cache_key_data.items()))
        aot_config.extra_cache_key_data = extra_data_sorted_by_keys

    return (
    # ...
```

Once we have the data collected and stored in a place we have access to it, it's time to wire it accordingly in the cache systems.

In the [`AOTAutogradCache.try_load`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/autograd_cache.py#L744) method, the extra data can be appended to the `fx_config: _CompileFxKwargs` object, [just before](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/autograd_cache.py#L764-L767) creation of the AOTCache key:

```python
class AOTAutogradCache(GuardedCache[GenericAOTAutogradResult[Any, Any]]):

    @staticmethod
    def try_load(
        # ...
    ) -> Callable[..., Any] | None:

        # ...

            fx_config: _CompileFxKwargs = {
                "cudagraphs": cudagraphs,
                "boxed_forward_device_index": boxed_forward_device_index,
            }

            # if there was provided extra_cache_key_data in aot_config, append it to the
            # _CompileFxKwargs, so it will be pickled when calculating cache key
            if aot_config.extra_cache_key_data is not None:
                fx_config["extra_cache_key_data"] = aot_config.extra_cache_key_data

        # ...

```

Now we also have to include in the Inductor's FxGraphCache. For the purposes of PoC for this RFC, I have passed the extra data to Inductor via `meta` of the graph_module under the `'extra_cache_key_data'` key, just before the [`aot_stage2_compile`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/15dbd457a8f7e15995e753e5d5ff3e04828711f4/torch/_functorch/aot_autograd.py#L1161):
```python
            # ...

            # if any extra cache key data is included in aot_config, pass it to the meta
            # of the graph module, so it will be accessible when preparing _CompileFxKwargs
            # for key cache calculations
            if aot_config.extra_cache_key_data is not None:
                aot_graph_capture.graph_module.meta['extra_cache_key_data'] = aot_config.extra_cache_key_data

            compiled_fn, _ = aot_stage2_compile(
            # ...
```

Having this data in `meta`, the extra data can be appended to the `fx_kwargs: _CompileFxKwargs` object in the [`FxGraphCache.prepare_key`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9fcc3ef74aebdd95635637a2bce5de98d4d9b66/torch/_inductor/codecache.py#L1618-L1620):

```python
class FxGraphCache(GuardedCache[CompiledFxGraph]):

    @staticmethod
    def prepare_key(
        # ...
    ) -> tuple[tuple[str, list[str]] | None, dict[str, Any]]:

        # ...

            # if there was provided extra_cache_key_data in gm.meta, append it to the
            # _CompileFxKwargs, so it will be pickled when calculating cache key
            if "extra_cache_key_data" in gm.meta:
                fx_kwargs["extra_cache_key_data"] = gm.meta["extra_cache_key_data"]

        # ...

```

This, together with DynamoCache hook, should be enough to equip the users with the ability of embedding their own custom validity checks regarding cached artifacts.

#### Opens

There are still some questions left to answer:

B.1) just like in the Dynamo case, we don't break the flow when the users' callback would throw, should we add some option to customize this behavior?

B.2) Another question is: right now we're propagating the extra data to Inductor's cache from the AOTAutograd hook - should we add a separate, 3rd hook, just for the Inductor's cache?

## **Notes / limitations**

By default, nothing changes in the framework's behavior, unless the proposed hooks are used.

This is a low-level extension point and is intentionally minimal.

Users providing their code to be used in those hooks, are responsible for ensuring the cache usage will be reasonable, for example that extra data provided for Inductor and AOTAutograd cache keys are deterministic and picklable.

cc @ezyang @EikanWang @jgong5 @wenzhe-nrv @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @jiayisunx @ipiszy @kadeng @muchulee8 @amjames @aakhundov @coconutruben @jataylo @azahed98 @bdhirsh @bobrenjc93 @aorenste @gujinghui @Lucaskabela

issues.body:
## Author - @fffrog - @can-gaa-hou - @KarhouTam ## Abstract This RFC proposes a cross-repo CI coordination mechanism based on a GitHub App and a Relay Server. The system allows specific events in the PyTorch repository to automatically trigger CI jobs in downstream repos. Based on configuration, results can optionally be reported back to the PyTorch PR check list or HUD, with support for hints, PR blocking, re-runs, and update notifications. This provides strong compatibility guarantees between PyTorch and its downstream repositories. > \[!NOTE\] > - This design does not guarantee 100% event delivery. > - Each downstream repo that uses this mechanism is the primary owner of its own CI failures. ## Architecture This design involves four core components: - **GitHub App:** The authentication and decoupling hub. It declares required permissions, event subscriptions, and handles authorization. - **PyTorch Repo:** The upstream event source. It authorizes external communication through the GitHub App. - **Relay Server:** The core dispatcher. It handles Webhook events from GitHub and callback requests from downstream repos. - **Downstream Repos:** The repos that actually run the tests (out-of-tree backend accelerator plugins). The overall flow and component responsibilities are shown below: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram actor Dev as Developer participant PT as PyTorch box rgba(36,41,47,0.08) GitHub Platform participant APP as GitHub App
(Auth Hub) participant API as GitHub API end box rgba(0,118,255,0.08) Relay Server participant GW as AWS API Gateway participant LM as AWS Lambda participant CH as ClickHouse end participant DS as Downstream Repo Dev->>PT: Create/Update PR / Re-run Check PT->>APP: Webhook Event
(PR opened/reopened/synchronize, Check rerequested) APP->>GW: POST /relay-webhook
(event payload) GW->>LM: Invoke Relay Handler Note over LM: Verify X-Hub-Signature-256
(Webhook Secret) Note over LM: Read YAML allowlist
from test-infra repo LM->>APP: Sign JWT with Private Key APP-->>LM: JWT LM->>API: Exchange JWT for Installation Access Token API-->>LM: Installation Access Token LM->>API: Query repos with App installed API-->>LM: Installed repo list Note over LM: Intersect installed repos ∩ allowlist (forward_event=true)
→ eligible downstream repos loop For each eligible downstream repo alt L4 OR (L3 AND PR has ciflow/oot/ label) LM->>API: Create in_progress Check Run API->>PT: PR Checks show "in progress" end LM->>API: repository_dispatch + payload (fire-and-forget) API->>DS: Trigger Workflow end Note over LM: (Optional) Write dispatch log to ClickHouse Note over DS: Pull PR code → Build → Test DS->>GW: POST /relay-callback
(conclusion + details URL) GW->>LM: Invoke Callback Handler Note over LM: Verify callback payload alt display_on_hud=true (L2+) LM->>CH: Write to oot_ci_results table (OOT HUD page) end alt L4 OR (L3 AND ciflow/oot/ label present) LM->>API: Request PyTorch Installation Token (via App identity) API-->>LM: Token alt L4 (block_pr=true) LM->>API: Update Check Run (blocking, failure blocks merge) else L3 with label (display_on_pr=label_only) LM->>API: Update Check Run (informational, non-blocking) end API->>PT: PR Checks updated with result end ``` ## GitHub App The GitHub App is the **authentication and decoupling hub** of the entire design. It plays three key roles: - **Unified identity:** The Relay Server calls the GitHub API as the GitHub App identity (not a personal PAT). The permission lifecycle is independent of any personal account, making it secure and manageable. - **Event bridge:** Through Webhook subscriptions, GitHub pushes PR events to the Relay Server in real time, driving the entire automation flow. - **Upstream/downstream decoupling:** Downstream repos **only need to install this App to join the cross-repo CI coordination**. Downstream repos do not need an upstream token, and the upstream does not need to know about the downstream. All interactions are bridged through the GitHub App and Relay Server. > \[!NOTE\] > This GitHub App should be created under the `pytorch` organization and owned by the PyTorch team or the LF AI & Data Foundation team, to ensure credibility. An App created by a third party will face trust issues during installation and adoption. ### Permissions / Events Following the principle of least privilege, the full set of permissions and event subscriptions required by the GitHub App is as follows: #### Permissions | Category | Permission | Level | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Repository | Actions | Read & Write | Re-run downstream CI workflows on demand; when a developer re-requests a Check Run on a GitHub PR page, the Relay Server can re-dispatch the OOT job | | Repository | Checks | Read & Write | Create/update Check Runs on PyTorch PRs to relay downstream CI status and conclusions | | Repository | Contents | Read & Write | Read repo content and config files; send `repository_dispatch` events to downstream repos to trigger CI workflows | | Repository | Pull requests | Read-only | Read PR metadata (branch, SHA, author, etc.) to build the downstream payload | | Repository | Metadata | Read-only | Required base permission for GitHub Apps | #### Events | Event | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | | Pull request | Trigger downstream CI when a PR is opened or reopened; clean up when a PR is closed | | Check suite | Handle re-run requests for all Check Runs within a Check Suite | | Check run | Handle re-run requests for a single Check Run | ### Key Configuration | Config | Description | | :--- | :--- | | **Webhook URL** | The public endpoint of the Relay Server. GitHub pushes all subscribed events here. | | **Webhook Secret** | A high-entropy random string. The Relay Server uses it to verify the request source and prevent forgery. | | **Private Key** | Download the `.pem` file after creation. The Relay Server uses it to generate a JWT for calling the GitHub API. **Must be stored securely and never committed to a code repository.** | | **Installation Scope** | Must be set to **"Any account"** (public installation). Downstream repos may belong to different organizations, and only a public installation can support cross-organization coordination. | ## PyTorch (Upstream) ### Installing the GitHub App After the GitHub App is created, a PyTorch repo Maintainer opens the App installation link in a browser, selects the `PyTorch` repository, and confirms the installation. ### Reusable Actions After a downstream repo receives the `repository_dispatch` event from the Relay Server, typical CI workflow steps are: 1. Pull the PyTorch PR source code based on PR info in the payload 2. Build PyTorch 3. Check out the downstream repo (using the existing `checkout` action) 4. Build the downstream plugin 5. Run tests 6. Report results to the Relay Server **Step 1** and **Step 6** are common needs shared by all downstream repos, and the logic is identical. To avoid requiring downstream repos to understand the Relay Server integration details (such as callback URLs and auth tokens), and to standardize the result reporting format, this proposal suggests creating two reusable Actions in the PyTorch repo for all downstream repos to reference directly. #### Action 1: `pytorch/.github/actions/checkout-pr` Checks out the PyTorch PR source code into the downstream workspace, based on PR metadata (PR number, head SHA, head ref, etc.) in the `repository_dispatch` event payload. This Action encapsulates all the logic for checking out PyTorch code. Downstream repos can use it directly without parsing the payload or running git commands themselves. #### Action 2: `pytorch/.github/actions/report-ci-result` Called as the last step of the downstream CI workflow to report standardized execution results to the Relay Server. This Action defines a structured format with required fields (e.g., `conclusion`, `details_url`) and optional fields (e.g., `summary`), ensuring all downstream repos output consistent, machine-readable results. The Relay Server then decides, based on the allowlist policy, whether to report the result back to the PyTorch PR as a Check Run. > \[!NOTE\] > This structured data is the source for the downstream repo's dedicated HUD page. It can be dynamically extended based on downstream repo requirements, including run results, downstream CI infrastructure status, and more. ## Relay Server The Relay Server is the core dispatcher. It handles two types of incoming requests and applies the allowlist policy: 1. **PR events from PyTorch** (Webhook push): Trigger CI in downstream repos 2. **Callbacks from downstream repos** (HTTP callback): Relay CI results back to the upstream PR ### Allowlist Policy The allowlist is the core control mechanism of the Relay Server. It determines how deeply each downstream repo participates. The Relay Server maintains the following fields for each downstream repo (repos not explicitly configured use default values): | Field | Type | Description | Default | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `forward_event` | bool | Controls whether upstream PR events are forwarded to this downstream repo. Acts as a gate to prevent abuse from unauthorized large-scale installations. | `false` | | `display_on_hud` | bool | Controls whether downstream CI results are shown on the dedicated OOT HUD page (`hud.pytorch.org/oot/[org]/[repo]`). | `false` | | `display_on_pr` | string | Controls whether downstream CI results can be shown as a Check Run in the **PR Checks** list.
**Options:**
`always`, `label_only`, `false` | `false` | | `block_pr` | bool | Controls whether the Check Run shown in **PR Checks** can block PR merges. | `false` | Based on these four fields, four participation levels are defined: | Level | forward_event | display_on_hud | display_on_pr | block_pr | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `L1` | `true` | `false` | `false` | `false` | Events are forwarded to downstream, but upstream receives no downstream feedback. | | `L2` | `true` | `true` | `false` | `false` | Downstream results are shown on the dedicated HUD page by default. | | `L3` | `true` | `true` | `label_only` | `false` | Adds a non-blocking Check Run for the device in PR Checks (only triggered when the `ciflow/oot/` label is added). | | `L4` | `true` | `true` | `always` | `true` | Adds a blocking Check Run for the device in PR Checks (auto-triggered for every PR); reserved for critical accelerators only. | > \[!NOTE\] > - Repos not listed in the allowlist YAML default to: no downstream CI triggered, no results forwarded, and no PR merges blocked. > - For L3, the `ciflow/oot/` label permission is enforced by the existing pytorchbot mechanism in PyTorch, which already prevents unauthorized users (non-PR authors or Maintainers) from adding `ciflow/oot/` labels to a PR. Level management is based on a YAML config file. Downstream repo developers who meet the requirements in the [Evolution Path](#evolution-path) section can submit a PR with supporting materials to modify this config file. Community Maintainers/TAC will review and merge it. ```yaml L1: - org1/repo1 - org2/repo2 L2: - org3/repo3 L3: - org4/repo4 L4: - org5/repo5: @oncall1,oncall2 ``` ### Evolution Path The allowlist is designed to naturally support gradual progression from experimental participation to mature participation, downstream repos that meet the requirements can apply to advance level by level (L1 → L2 → L3 → L4). The table below lists the requirements for advancing to each level. | Phase | Level | Requirements | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Onboarding** | `L1` | 1. GitHub App installed
2. Provide verifiable accelerator hardware information
3. Provide a downstream adaptation repo for the accelerator | | **Observation** | `L2` | 1. Follow the standard [Workflow Configuration](#workflow-configuration) to receive events and report results
2. Must not send excessive or invalid requests to the Relay Server | | **Stable** | `L3` | 1. CI infrastructure must keep job queue time under `X min` per workflow
2. CI infrastructure must keep total run time under `X hour` per PR
3. Weekly CI success rate > `X %` (including both infra failures and test failures) | | **Mature** | `L4` | Fully determined by Core Maintainer, considering factors including but not limited to:
- `community adoption`,
- `hardware usage`,
- `test coverage` (whether the PyTorch core test suite is required, @mikaylagawarecki),
- `test pass rate`,
- `oncall responsiveness`, etc. | > \[!NOTE\] > - The requirements above are an **initial reference** and may **be adjusted over time based on real-world conditions** (e.g., determining the specific values of `X`). > - To maintain the PyTorch community's user experience, **downstream repos that no longer meet the requirements of their current level will be downgraded to the level that matches their actual status.** > - `L3` is the recommended long-term target for most downstream repos, as it provides a good balance between signal depth and minimal negative impact on upstream. > - `L4`: Only applies to a small number of downstream repos. Detailed requirements will be defined before any backend approaches the `L4` bar. ## Downstream Repos ### Installation After the GitHub App is created, downstream repos that want to receive PyTorch PR events open the App installation link in a browser, select the target repo or organization, and confirm. This completes the downstream repo's authorization of the GitHub App. ### Relay Configuration Downstream developers follow the requirements in the [Evolution Path](#evolution-path) section and submit a PR to the [test-infra](https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra) repo with supporting evidence (e.g., accelerator details, CI reliability metrics). After a community Maintainer reviews and merges it, the Relay Server will forward events according to the updated config. ### Workflow Configuration Downstream backend CI workflows share a similar structure: pull upstream code, build, test, and report results. Below is a reference template showing the key steps. Each backend can add intermediate steps as needed. ```yaml name: PyTorch CI on: repository_dispatch: types: [pytorch-pr-trigger] concurrency: group: upstream-pr-${{ github.event.client_payload.pr_number }} cancel-in-progress: true jobs: upstream-ci: runs-on: [self-hosted] steps: # Step 1: Report the startup status to the relay server so that a check run with a status of "In Progress" can be created for the PR - name: Report startup to Relay Server uses: pytorch/actions/report-ci-result@v1 if: always() # Must report regardless of success or failure with: conclusion: ${{ job.status }} url: ${{ github.server_url }}/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }} # other parameters... # Step 2: Check out PyTorch PR code - name: Checkout PyTorch PR uses: pytorch/actions/checkout-pr@v1 with: head-sha: ${{ github.event.client_payload.head_sha }} path: pytorch # Check out to ./pytorch directory # Step 3: Build PyTorch - name: Build PyTorch working-directory: pytorch run: | pip3 install -vvv --no-build-isolation -e . # Example only # Step 4: Check out downstream repo - name: Checkout downstream repo uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: path: backend # Step 5: Build backend plugin - name: Build backend working-directory: backend run: | python setup.py develop # Step 6: Run tests - name: Test backend run: | pytest tests/ # Step 7: Report results to Relay Server - name: Report CI result uses: pytorch/actions/report-ci-result@v1 if: always() # Must report regardless of success or failure with: conclusion: ${{ job.status }} url: ${{ github.server_url }}/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }} # other parameters... ``` ## HUD Integration The PyTorch CI HUD (hud.pytorch.org) is a CI status dashboard maintained by the PyTorch team. It shows all CI job runs for every commit and PR. To minimize the impact of downstream repo results on the PyTorch HUD, this proposal introduces the following HUD integration strategy: - **Dedicated OOT repo page (`hud.pytorch.org/oot/[org]/[repo]`):** Available from L2 onwards. Downstream CI results are shown on a dedicated page for the downstream repo. The layout is similar to the main HUD page, but focused only on the test history of a single downstream repo. It gives OOT Maintainers a self-service CI health dashboard without affecting any upstream views. - **Global OOT CI summary page:** Primarily for PyTorch CI Maintainers. Provides a global view of OOT CI health across all repos. Makes it easy to spot widespread OOT infrastructure issues or identify repos that may need to be downgraded. - **HUD PR view (`hud.pytorch.org/pr/`):** For L3/L4 repos, OOT check results are displayed in the PR-level HUD view under a dedicated "Out-of-Tree Backends" section, grouped alongside standard CI results. This ensures developers and Maintainers can see OOT CI status in their normal PR review workflow without switching to a separate page. - **Main HUD page:** Only shows `L4` (required) Check Runs, ensuring the main dashboard stays focused on signals that every PyTorch contributor needs to care about. The Relay Server writes all results from `L2` and above into `ClickHouse`, which powers the dedicated OOT HUD pages described above. ## Alternative Architecture The design described in the [Architecture](#architecture) section processes webhook events and downstream fan-out synchronously within a single Lambda invocation. While straightforward, this means that if the Lambda encounters a transient failure mid-dispatch (e.g., GitHub API rate limit spike, network timeout), some downstream repos may miss the event with no built-in retry mechanism. This RFC therefore proposes a more resilient alternative architecture: The webhook handler only performs signature verification and task persistence (writing dispatch tasks to DynamoDB), returning a `202 Accepted` immediately. DynamoDB Streams then trigger separate Lambda invocations for asynchronous fan-out, providing built-in retry semantics, per-task isolation, and reliable at-least-once delivery to all eligible downstream repos. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram actor Dev as Developer participant PT as PyTorch box rgba(36,41,47,0.08) GitHub Platform participant APP as GitHub App
(Auth Hub) participant API as GitHub API end box rgba(0,118,255,0.08) Relay Server participant V as Vercel API Route participant DB as DynamoDB participant LM as AWS Lambda participant CH as ClickHouse end participant DS as Downstream Repo Dev->>PT: Create/Update PR / Re-run Check PT->>APP: Webhook Event
(PR opened/reopened/synchronize, Check rerequested) APP->>V: Webhook push → /api/relay/webhook
(event payload) Note over V: Verify X-Hub-Signature-256
(Webhook Secret) V->>DB: Write to relay-dispatch-tasks V-->>APP: Return 202 Accepted (< 3s) Note over LM: Asynchronous Fan-out (Max 15 min) DB->>LM: DynamoDB Streams trigger LM->>APP: Sign JWT with Private Key APP-->>LM: JWT LM->>API: Exchange JWT for Installation Access Token API-->>LM: Installation Access Token LM->>API: Query repos with App installed API-->>LM: Installed repo list Note over LM: Intersect installed repos ∩ allowlist (forward_event=true)
→ eligible downstream repos loop For each eligible downstream repo alt L4 OR (L3 AND PR has ciflow/oot/ label) LM->>API: Create in_progress Check Run API->>PT: PR Checks show "in progress" end LM->>API: repository_dispatch + payload API->>DS: Trigger Workflow end Note over DS: Pull PR code → Build → Test DS->>V: Callback → /api/relay/callback
(conclusion + details URL) Note over V: Verify callback payload alt display_on_hud=true (L2+) V->>CH: Write to oot_ci_results table (OOT HUD page) end alt L4 OR (L3 AND ciflow/oot/ label present) V->>API: Request PyTorch Installation Token (via App identity) API-->>V: Token alt L4 (block_pr=true) V->>API: Update Check Run (blocking, failure blocks merge) else L3 with label (display_on_pr=label_only) V->>API: Update Check Run (informational, non-blocking) end API->>PT: PR Checks updated with result end ``` ## Demo An end-to-end prototype has been completed. A few key points are noted below. 1. Upstream repo — Checks overview - To avoid cluttering the PyTorch PR Checks page, the naming convention for Check Runs is defined as `oot / DEVICE / workflow detail`. With this naming, related checks are automatically grouped alphabetically in the UI. - By configuring `concurrency` in the downstream workflow, when a PR is updated, the old Action is cancelled and a new one runs. The upstream Check Run is updated accordingly. 2. Upstream repo — Check Run details - The right-hand detail panel can be customized to show the `downstream Action link`, `run result`, and `key errors` (can be extended later as needed). - Clicking `Re-run` or `Re-run checks` will trigger the downstream Action to re-run, and the new result will automatically sync back to the upstream Check Run. ## Security Considerations - **Webhook signature verification:** The Relay Server must verify the `X-Hub-Signature-256` header on every Webhook request to confirm the request comes from GitHub and prevent third-party event forgery. - **Callback authentication:** When a downstream repo sends a callback result to the Relay Server, the server must verify the legitimacy of the request (e.g., validate the PR / Check Run ID in the payload) to prevent malicious repos from injecting fake CI results into upstream PRs. - **Token expiry:** GitHub App Installation Access Tokens are valid for 1 hour. The Relay Server should request them on demand and discard them immediately after use, with no long-term caching, to minimize the impact window of a token leak.

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

**Title**  
[Feature Request] `torch.autograd.cut_gradient(loss, cut_at)` — per-loss selective upstream gradient blocking with **zero extra memory / zero extra compute**

**Is this a feature request or a bug report?** Feature request

**Description**

### Problem / Motivation

Many models share a computation graph up to an intermediate tensor, then branch into multiple losses where each loss should affect *different subsets* of the network.

**Concrete example** (the exact pattern we hit constantly):

```python
state2 = backbone(input)          # expensive shared encoder / W1
hidden3 = later_shared(state2)    # W2 / decoder / shared head
loss1 = head1(hidden3, target1)   # Task 1 — should update EVERYTHING (backbone + later_shared + head1)
loss2 = head2(hidden3, target2)   # Task 2 — should update ONLY from state2 onward (NO gradients into backbone/W1)
```

Desired behavior (single forward, single backward, one optimizer):
- `W1/backbone` receives gradient **only from loss1**
- Everything from `state2` onward receives `loss1 + loss2`
- **No `retain_graph=True`** (kills peak memory on large models)
- **No second forward pass** on `later_shared` with a detached copy
- **No manual `grad` + subtract**, no temporary `requires_grad=False`, no extra compute

### Current workarounds and why they are unacceptable

1. `loss1.backward(retain_graph=True); loss2.backward()` → peak memory spike (full graph kept alive)
2. `state2_det = state2.detach(); hidden3_2 = later_shared(state2_det); loss2 = ...` → wastes compute & memory on duplicate forward
3. `torch.autograd.grad(loss2, backbone.parameters())` + manual `.sub_()` → still requires `retain_graph=True` on first backward + extra compute
4. Temporarily `requires_grad=False` on W1 → brittle, error-prone with complex modules/optimizers

When memory is the bottleneck (large backbones, long sequences, high batch size, etc.), **none of these are viable**.

### Proposed API (primary recommendation)

```python
loss2_cut = torch.autograd.cut_gradient(loss2, cut_at=state2)   # or cut_at=[state2, ...]

total_loss = loss1 + loss2_cut
total_loss.backward()          # ← normal single backward, no retain_graph, optimal memory & speed

optimizer.step()
```

**Alternative general API** (if the team prefers one call):

```python
torch.autograd.backward_with_cuts([
    (loss1, None),           # no cuts
    (loss2, state2),         # cut upstream of state2 for this loss
])
```

**Or as Tensor method** (nice ergonomics):

```python
loss2_cut = loss2.detach_upstream(state2)
```

### Minimal reproducible example (for testing)

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

backbone = nn.Linear(10, 20)
later = nn.Linear(20, 30)
head1 = nn.Linear(30, 5)
head2 = nn.Linear(30, 5)

x = torch.randn(8, 10)
t1 = torch.randn(8, 5)
t2 = torch.randn(8, 5)

state2 = backbone(x)
hidden3 = later(state2)

l1 = (head1(hidden3) - t1).pow(2).mean()
l2 = (head2(hidden3) - t2).pow(2).mean()

# === with proposed feature ===
l2_cut = torch.autograd.cut_gradient(l2, cut_at=state2)
total = l1 + l2_cut
total.backward()

# Expected:
#   backbone.weight.grad comes only from l1
#   later.weight.grad comes from l1 + l2

### Why this matters (use cases)

- Multi-task / multi-head learning where auxiliary losses must not pollute the shared encoder
- Hierarchical / modular networks
- Actor-critic RL (value loss should not update early policy layers)
- Knowledge distillation / auxiliary prediction heads with controlled gradient flow
- Any time you want “one loss affects the whole model, another loss affects only downstream of X”

This is a **very common pattern** that currently has no first-class, zero-overhead solution.

### Implementation notes

The autograd engine already has the full DAG. We only need to:
- Tag gradient contributions by their originating loss root, or
- Insert a lightweight “CutGradFn” node that knows which root it belongs to and zeros upstream flow for that root only.

This would be analogous to `torch.no_grad` / `detach` but scoped to a specific loss root.

**Impact**: Huge win for memory-constrained training (large models, long contexts, high batch) and cleaner code for the entire community.

**Suggested labels**: `module: autograd`, `feature`, `triaged`
```

### Alternatives

### Current workarounds and why they are unacceptable

1. `loss1.backward(retain_graph=True); loss2.backward()` → peak memory spike (full graph kept alive)
2. `state2_det = state2.detach(); hidden3_2 = later_shared(state2_det); loss2 = ...` → wastes compute & memory on duplicate forward
3. `torch.autograd.grad(loss2, backbone.parameters())` + manual `.sub_()` → still requires `retain_graph=True` on first backward + extra compute
4. Temporarily `requires_grad=False` on W1 → brittle, error-prone with complex modules/optimizers

When memory is the bottleneck (large backbones, long sequences, high batch size, etc.), **none of these are viable**.


### Additional context

_No response_

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

torch/testing/_internal/common_cuda.py -- and elsewhere throughout the unit tests -- contains code such as 

```python
SM53OrLater = LazyVal(lambda: torch.cuda.is_available() and torch.cuda.get_device_capability() >= (5, 3))
IS_JETSON = LazyVal(lambda: torch.cuda.is_available() and (torch.cuda.get_device_capability() in [(7, 2), (8, 7)] or IS_THOR))
```
On ROCm and other platforms, querying device capability is abstract.  The intent is to verify at runtime whether your current accelerator hardware supports a certain feature, whether it be a data type or something else.  There is an effort to [support accelerator device capabilities](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/169277), but those are currently limited to only querying supported data types.

The torch/testing/ and test/ directories need to be audited for uses of get_device_capability() and replaced with generic accelerator feature queries.  The rationale for using the device capability should be captured in a self-documenting LazyVal or function.

Here's an example not using get_device_capability(), instead it parses HIP version and demonstrates a self-documenting variable to represent a feature rather than abstract integer.  This could be extended to additional accelerators to represent a generic feature of SPMM_COMPLEX128_SUPPORTED.

```python
CUSPARSE_SPMM_COMPLEX128_SUPPORTED = (
    IS_WINDOWS and torch.version.cuda
) or (not IS_WINDOWS and not TEST_WITH_ROCM)

HIPSPARSE_SPMM_COMPLEX128_SUPPORTED = torch.version.hip and version.parse(torch.version.hip.split("-")[0]) >= version.parse("6.0")
```

This proposed feature is targeting the various unit test files within pytorch.  Related to, but outside the scope of this proposal, is to audit the C++ sources shared by CUDA/ROCm for uses of device capability queries and handle them in a similar way.

### Alternatives

_No response_

It used to be that you couldn't use SAC over a torch.compile region. This was especially annoying for usage of flex attention.

Now, it kind of works with:

```
torch._inductor.config.wrap_inductor_compiled_regions = True
```

However, when you write your policy function, something annoying happens. If you wrote your policy function to be matching on op names (pretty common), you end up having to match on "inductor_compiled_code" instead of something sensible like "flex_attention". This is bad.

I'm not sure what I want the alternative to be. I think for flex attention, I would like the HOP to "live on" in the resulting compiled region. But this would be weirdly special-casey, because normally the flex attention HOP is /inside/ the compiled region and is completely vaporized by the act of compilation. It feels almost as if the compile region should be /inside/ the HOP somehow. Not sure if you can actually do that.

There's also some more grungy ways of fixing it, like forcing people to stick their grubby hands into the HOP and read out the info they need, e.g., some extra metadata field or literally looking at the ops on the uncompiled graph to figure something out.

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Background
PyTorch currently disallows negative-step slicing (e.g. `x[::-1]`, `x[..., ::-k]`) and raises `ValueError: step must be greater than zero` (see #59786, #165244).
```python
>>> import torch

>>> tensor = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3])
>>> tensor[::-1]
ValueError: step must be greater than zero
```
Historically, `torch.flip()` has been suggested as a workaround (at least for `::-1`). However, for `k > 1` and especially when combined with indexing tuples (`...`, `None`/newaxis, multiple sliced dims), manually rewriting `[::-k]` into a sequence of ops is verbose and error-prone. In practice users often reach for patterns like “slice-then-flip” (e.g. `x[::k].flip(dim)`), which can silently diverge from NumPy semantics depending on shape/step, and becomes harder to reason about with `...` / `None`. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/59786#issuecomment-1364118843

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> x = np.arange(10)
>>> x[::-2]
array([9, 7, 5, 3, 1])

>>> y = torch.arange(10)
>>> y[::2].flip(dims=(0,))
tensor([8, 6, 4, 2, 0])

>>> y[1::2].flip(dims=(0,))
tensor([9, 7, 5, 3, 1])
```
Also note that `torch.flip` makes a copy (unlike NumPy `np.flip`, which can return a view), so it’s useful but not an ideal drop-in mental model for slicing. https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/38271


### Proposal
* support `slice(None, None, -k)` as syntactic sugar by rewriting it internally to `flip` + positive-step slicing:
  * `x[..., ::-k]` → `x.flip(dim)[..., ::k]` (for each affected dim)
* This improves user ergonomics and helps downstream Array API users, while keeping implementation localized and avoiding negative-stride views.
* This proposal only covers `slice(None, None, -k)`

### Alternatives

use `torch.flip()` : https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/59786#issuecomment-1364118843

### Additional context

### Related Issue and Ref:
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/229
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/165244
- https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/API_specification/indexing.html#slice-syntax
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/59786#issuecomment-1364118843
- https://github.com/data-apis/array-api-compat/issues/144
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/59786
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/38271
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/58743

### Related File:
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/csrc/autograd/python_variable_indexing.cpp
- https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/aten/src/ATen/TensorIndexing.cpp

Please let me know if I’ve misunderstood anything.
Thank you.

issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Summary

This RFC proposes adding a cuTile backend to PyTorch Inductor, providing a complementary CUDA code generation path using the cuTile library. This would enable the broader community to benefit from Tile IR's bytecode portability, performance portability across GPU generations, and access to an optimizing compiler specifically designed for tile-based GPU programming. We have a working implementation that can be contributed in phases to facilitate review and integration.

## Motivation

PyTorch Inductor currently uses Triton as the primary backend for CUDA code generation. We propose adding a cuTile backend as a complementary path that leverages a hardware-aligned tile-based programming model.

**What is cuTile?**
[cuTile](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cutile-python/#) is a Python library targeting [Tile IR](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/tile-ir/latest/index.html), a virtual instruction set enabling native, portable tile-based GPU programming.

**Why This Matters:**
- **Hardware & Performance Portability**: cuTile targets Tile IR, a virtual ISA analogous to PTX. This abstraction decouples kernel logic from specific hardware, allowing kernels (e.g., GEMM, attention) to be "written once" and re-targeted to different architectures. It ensures optimized performance across multiple GPU generations via compiler-level mapping rather than manual kernel rewrites.
- **Enabling Higher-Level DSLs**: [Helion](https://github.com/pytorch/helion) is a Python-embedded DSL for authoring ML kernels that currently compiles to Triton. We are planning to add a Tile IR/cuTile backend to Helion; implementing Inductor cuTile support is a necessary prerequisite for this path, as it provides the foundational infrastructure required for Helion to target Tile IR.
- **Competitive Performance**: cuTile provides performance competitive to cuBLAS for GEMMs and cuDNN for attention at large problem sizes.

## Proposed Design

### Architecture Overview

We propose integrating the cuTile backend into Inductor's existing architecture at the code generation layer, maintaining symmetry with the current Triton implementation:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    PyTorch FX Graph                         │
└─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Inductor IR (Pointwise, Reduction)             │
└─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                      │
                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Scheduler & Fusion                         │
└─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                      │
         ┌────────────┴────────────┐
         ▼                         ▼
┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐
│  Triton Backend  │      │  cuTile Backend  │
│  (tl.* APIs)     │      │  (ct.* APIs)     │
└──────────────────┘      └──────────────────┘
         │                         │
         ▼                         ▼
┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐
│  Triton JIT      │      │  cuTile JIT      │
│  Compiler        │      │  Compiler        │
└──────────────────┘      └──────────────────┘
         │                         │
         └────────────┬────────────┘
                      ▼
              ┌───────────────┐
              │  CUDA Kernels │
              └───────────────┘
```

### Key Components

#### 1. Backend Selection (`torch/_inductor/config.py`)

Users select cuTile via configuration:
```python
torch._inductor.config.cuda_backend = "cutile"
```
To ensure a seamless and stable integration:

- **Opt-in only**: Triton remains the default backend for all CUDA code generation. When `cuda_backend = "triton"` (the default), cuTile code paths are never imported or invoked, ensuring zero overhead for existing users.
- **Automatic Fallback**: If the cuTile backend encounters an unsupported operation, it automatically falls back to the ATen path. This ensures that models always execute correctly even as native operator coverage in cuTile expands.

**Usage Example:**
```python
import torch

torch._inductor.config.cuda_backend = "cutile"

@torch.compile
def my_fn(x, y):
    return torch.softmax(x + y, dim=-1)

x = torch.randn(1024, 2048, device='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16)
y = torch.randn(1024, 2048, device='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16)
result = my_fn(x, y)
```

#### 2. Code Generation & Class Refactoring

We introduce a **TileKernel abstraction layer** to generalize tile-based codegen, allowing logic sharing between Triton and cuTile.

- **TileKernel / TileKernelScheduling (NEW)**: Base classes for all tile-aware backends
- **TritonKernel / TritonScheduling (REFACTORED)**: Now inherit from the Tile base classes
- **CutileKernel / CutileScheduling (NEW)**: Implementation of ct.* API generation
- **TileTemplateMixin (NEW)**: Shared template logic used by both `TritonTemplateKernel` and `CutileTemplateKernel`

**Hierarchy Diagrams:**

```
Kernel Classes:
SIMDKernel
└── TileKernel (NEW)
    ├── TritonKernel (REFACTORED)
    └── CutileKernel (NEW)

Template Kernels:
TileTemplateMixin (NEW)
├── TritonTemplateKernel = TileTemplateMixin + TritonKernel (REFACTORED)
└── CutileTemplateKernel = TileTemplateMixin + CutileKernel (NEW)

Scheduling:
SIMDScheduling
└── TileKernelScheduling (NEW)
    ├── TritonScheduling (REFACTORED)
    └── CutileScheduling (NEW)
```

#### 3. Runtime Helpers (`torch/_inductor/runtime/`)

Following the same pattern as Triton's runtime helpers:

**`cutile_heuristics.py`**: Autotuning heuristics for tile sizes, thread block configurations, and performance tuning

**`cutile_helpers.py`**: Runtime helper utilities for cuTile, analogous to `triton_helpers` for Triton. Includes common operations used by generated kernels (e.g., Welford online algorithms, nan-propagating min/max reductions) as well as pointer-based memory operations (`load_offset`, `store_offset`, `atomic_add_offset`). The pointer operations bridge the gap between Inductor's offset-based IR and cuTile's array-based model -- cuTile's native load/store APIs operate on arrays, which are not a natural target for Inductor's codegen. These pointer operations are implemented using internal cuTile APIs that are not part of the public stable interface and may break across cuda-tile releases. In the short term, we mitigate this through version pinning. Longer term, we plan to work with the cuTile team to either stabilize these APIs or introduce public pointer-based alternatives that align with Inductor's IR model.

### Scope & Fallback Behavior

The cuTile backend supports the following operation categories:
- **Pointwise**: arithmetic, logical, bitwise, comparisons, type conversions, etc.
- **Reductions**: sum, prod, mean, max, min, softmax, etc.
- **Matrix multiplication**: mm with autotuning
- **Scatter**: scatter_add, scatter_reduce, index_put
- **Memory**: transpose, permute, expand, clone, cat, etc.

Operations not yet supported fall back automatically to ATen eager mode. Current fallbacks include:
- **Extern-dependent ops**: functions requiring libdevice or external math libraries (e.g., acos, erf, lgamma)
- **Ops lacking native support**: randn, sort, scan

Operator coverage will expand incrementally across Phase 1 PRs.


### System Requirements

- **GPU**: Blackwell (SM 10.0+) currently; Future versions will add support for more architectures.
- **Python Package**: `cuda-tile` (via `pip install cuda-tile`)

## Roadmap & Upstreaming

We have developed an internal implementation and propose contributing it to PyTorch in phases.

**Phase 1: Initial Integration**
- Scope: Infrastructure (backend, config, helpers, autotuning, scheduling), Operations (pointwise, reductions, memory), Templates support, Tests & Documentation
- Phase 1 will be delivered as a series of PRs to keep reviews manageable, starting with infrastructure and copy kernels, then expanding to pointwise, reductions, templates, and GEMM
- Deliverables: Core operation support, fallback mechanism, Blackwell compatibility
- Success criteria: All tests pass on Blackwell, no Triton regressions
- Testing and CI Validation: We will leverage the existing Inductor test suite to validate the cuTile backend for functional parity with the ATen and Triton paths. Although cuda-tile is an optional dependency, we propose installing it in the PyTorch CI pipelines to ensure continuous verification of the codegen logic and to prevent regressions. While Blackwell hardware availability in CI is currently limited, we will perform internal validation on Blackwell nodes to ensure execution correctness.

**Phase 2 & Beyond:**
- **Short-term (1-2 releases)**: Expand operators (scan/sort, complex trig, random), fusion with templates, tuned heuristics
- **Medium-term**: Flash Attention, support for more GPUs
- **Long-term**: Post-Blackwell architectures, multi-backend autotuning

### Code Organization

**New files:**
```
torch/_inductor/codegen/cutile.py
torch/_inductor/codegen/cutile_utils.py
torch/_inductor/runtime/cutile_helpers.py
torch/_inductor/runtime/cutile_heuristics.py
torch/_inductor/codegen/cutile_combined_scheduling.py
test/inductor/test_cutile_backend.py
```


## Risks and Mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|------|-----------|
| **cuTile API changes** | Version pinning; internal API usage isolated to a single module (`cutile_helpers.py`); working with cuTile team on stable alternatives |
| **Performance regressions** | Keep Triton default |
| **Incomplete operator coverage** | Automatic ATen fallback; incremental expansion |
| **Maintenance burden** | Shared infrastructure with Triton; comprehensive tests |

- [cuTile Documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cutile-python/#)

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Summary
When an `fx.GraphModule` contains a TorchScript submodule (created via `torch.jit.script`), calling `GraphModule.to_folder()` fails because `torch.save` cannot pickle the TorchScript object. This blocks workflows that combine FX transforms with TorchScript-optimized submodules. A feature to support or gracefully handle TorchScript submodules during `to_folder()` would help.

## Environment
- Python: 3.10.19 (conda-forge, GCC 14.3.0)
- OS: Linux-6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 (WSL2)
- PyTorch: 2.5.1
- CUDA: 12.4

## Minimal reproduction
Save this as `repro_fx_torchscript_save.py` and run with `python repro_fx_torchscript_save.py`.

```python
import tempfile
import torch
from torch import fx, nn

class M(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(3, 4, 3, padding=1)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.conv(x)

m = M().eval()
gm = fx.symbolic_trace(m)

# Replace a submodule with a TorchScript version
scripted = torch.jit.script(gm.get_submodule("conv"))
setattr(gm, "conv", scripted)

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    gm.to_folder(tmp, "repro")
```

## Actual result
```
RuntimeError: Tried to serialize object __torch__.torch.nn.modules.conv.Conv2d which does not have a __getstate__ method defined!
```

## Expected result
`GraphModule.to_folder()` should either:
- support serializing TorchScript submodules (e.g. via `torch.jit.save`), or
- offer a documented fallback strategy (skip/replace/save separately) so mixed FX + TorchScript workflows can be persisted.

## Why this matters
FX transforms are useful for graph-level mutation, while TorchScript is useful for optimization. Today, combining them makes `to_folder()` unusable for persistence. A supported save path would enable more realistic tooling around FX-based model transformation.


### Alternatives

One alternative is to avoid attaching TorchScript modules to a GraphModule and instead keep everything as regular nn.Module instances. However, this defeats the purpose of combining FX graph transforms with
TorchScript-optimized components.

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

When a vmapped function returns a pytree containing non-tensor values (ints, strings, metadata), vmap raises ValueError: must only return Tensors. Non-tensor leaves were never batched and should pass through unchanged — this is what `jax.vmap` does.

```python
def f(x):
    return {"tensor": x.sin(), "count": 42}

torch.vmap(f)(torch.randn(4, 3))

ValueError
````

This forces users to convert all metadata to 0-d tensors, which is fragile and adds overhead.

### Implementation

In _unwrap_batched (torch/_functorch/vmap.py), after broadcasting out_dims to match the output tree structure, override out_dim to None for any leaf that isn't a torch.Tensor. This makes _maybe_remove_batch_dim pass them through instead of raising. The legacy path in torch/_vmap_internals.py gets the same treatment: _validate_outputs stops rejecting non-tensors, and _unwrap_batched skips _remove_batch_dim for non-tensor leaves.

issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

`torch.while_loop` has no `vmap` batching rule.

It raises `KeyError(TransformType.Vmap)` when called inside `torch.vmap`. Other higher-order ops (`cond`, `scan`) have `vmap` rules but `while_loop` does not.

```python
def fn(x):
    return torch.while_loop(lambda x: x.sum() < 10, lambda x: (x + 1,), (x,))

torch.vmap(fn)(torch.randn(4, 3))  # KeyError
```

This forces users to fall back to fixed-iteration for loops under vmap, running `max_iter` steps even when most batch elements converge in 3–5. For physics solvers this is a massive burden.

### Feature implementation

Register a `TransformType.Vmap` implementation on `while_loop_op`, following the same pattern as `cond` and `scan`. The rule unwraps batched inputs, expands any unbatched carried inputs to the batch size (with `.contiguous()` to match body output strides), then runs the loop with two wrappers: `wrapped_cond_fn` calls `restore_vmap` on the user's `cond_fn` and reduces the per-element booleans with `.any()`; `wrapped_body_fn` calls `restore_vmap` on `body_fn` and uses `torch.where(active_mask, new_val, old_val)` to freeze converged elements. The loop runs until all batch elements are done.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary**

TorchInductor currently lacks a proper abstraction for custom passes that operate on Loop‑level IR (List[BaseSchedulerNode]).

This results in incorrect cache classification and forces IR‑level passes such as _pre_fusion_custom_pass to inherit from CustomGraphPass, which is designed only for FX graph transformations.

This issue proposes introducing a new base class, CustomIRPass, to correctly represent and register Loop‑level IR passes and restore expected cache hit/miss behavior.

**Background & Motivation**

1. Abstraction mismatch

-  _pre_fusion_custom_pass operates directly on Loop‑level IR scheduler nodes.
- However, due to lack of an appropriate base class, it is currently forced to subclass CustomGraphPass, which applies to torch.fx.Graph transformations.
- This causes conceptual inconsistency.

2. Incorrect cache classification

- Inductor’s caching logic recognizes only CustomGraphPass.
- As a result, IR‑level passes implemented as subclasses of CustomGraphPass are treated as unsupported callables, making Inductor skip caching entirely.
- This led to avoidable cache misses during Intel PerfCore IPEX analysis.

3. Preserving uuid‑based caching guarantees

- Custom passes contribute to deterministic cache keys via uuid().
- IR‑level passes must implement this without depending on FX‑specific base class.


**Proposed Solution**
**Introduce a new abstraction: CustomIRPass**
A dedicated base class for Loop‑level IR transformations that will:
- Provide the correct abstraction for Loop‑level IR changes
- Register IR‑passes cleanly within Inductor
- Ensure cache logic properly recognizes IR‑level custom passes
- Maintain deterministic uuid() logic
- Clearly separate FX‑level and IR‑level transformation flows

Update _pre_fusion_custom_pass
- Modify it to inherit from the newly introduced CustomIRPass.


**Benefits**
- Restores correct TorchInductor cache hit/miss behavior
- Improves maintainability for custom IR passes
- Reduces unnecessary recompilation in Intel PerfCore IPEX workflows and similar environments

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

When exporting torch.affine_grid_generator to ONNX, I would prefer to use AffineGrid if possible. Additionally, what I'm ultimately curious about is whether there's a way to properly export the affine_grid_generator when its size has a dynamic shape.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def forward(self, theta, some_target):
        return torch.affine_grid_generator(theta, some_target.shape, align_corners=True)


model = Model()
theta = torch.ones((1, 2, 3))
some_target = torch.ones((1, 3, 512, 512))

torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic(some_target, 1)
torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic(some_target, 2)
torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic(some_target, 3)

torch.onnx.export(
    model,
    (theta, some_target),
    'test.onnx',
    opset_version=20,
)
```

After reading only the ONNX operation spec, I don't quite understand the reason for the dynamic shape constraint. Is this a constraint of the Torch-exported program?

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

```python
import onnx
from onnx import helper, TensorProto


def build_affine_grid_sample(
    opset: int = 20,
    align_corners: int = 1,
    padding_mode: str = "border",
) -> onnx.ModelProto:
    input_src = helper.make_tensor_value_info(
        "src", TensorProto.FLOAT, ["N", "C", "Hs", "Ws"]
    )
    input_dst = helper.make_tensor_value_info(
        "dst", TensorProto.FLOAT, ["N", "C", "Hd", "Wd"]
    )
    input_theta = helper.make_tensor_value_info(
        "theta", TensorProto.FLOAT, ["N", 2, 3]
    )
    output_out = helper.make_tensor_value_info(
        "out", TensorProto.FLOAT, ["N", "C", "Hd", "Wd"]
    )

    nodes = [
        helper.make_node("Shape", ["dst"], ["size"]),
        helper.make_node(
            "AffineGrid",
            ["theta", "size"],
            ["grid"],
            align_corners=align_corners,
        ),
        helper.make_node(
            "GridSample",
            ["src", "grid"],
            ["out"],
            align_corners=align_corners,
            mode="linear",
            padding_mode=padding_mode,
        ),
    ]

    graph = helper.make_graph(
        nodes,
        "AffineGridSample",
        [input_src, input_dst, input_theta],
        [output_out],
    )
    model = helper.make_model(
        graph,
        opset_imports=[helper.make_opsetid("", opset)],
        producer_name="affine_grid_sample",
    )
    onnx.checker.check_model(model)
    return model

model = build_affine_grid_sample(opset=20, align_corners=1)
onnx.save(model, "affine_grid_sample.onnx")
```

It would potentially be great to have a polar decomposition implemented in PyTorch.
Polar decomposition is useful in applications like Graphics, Vision, Quantum Computing, among others.
It can be used as an alternative to the Newton-Schulz step in the popular Muon optimizer (https://kellerjordan.github.io/posts/muon/). In general, it is a useful tool for orthogonalization.

cuSOLVER is to offer an implementation of the QR-based Dynamically Weighted Halley (QDWH) algorithm (proposed in https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/090774999, but adapted for HPC).
JAX exposes the algorithm directly, see https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/_autosummary/jax.lax.linalg.qdwh.html and https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/main/jax/_src/tpu/linalg/qdwh.py#L121 (I assume it follows https://www.netlib.org/utk/people/JackDongarra/PAPERS/task-polor-sc23.pdf).

The algorithm can expose the SVD decomposition (see https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/120876605). Conversely, the SVD can be used to derive the polar decomposition, but that inflicts a significant performance cost (in complexity and memory).

The decomposition is not hard to implement the JVP/VJP rules for, so it can be brought to the same level of integration as other `torch.linalg` operations.
