This feature request applies to both eager as well as non compiled autograd torch.compile. The problem is essentially: suppose a weight is used multiple times (e.g., due to microbatching), and you would like to fuse the accumulate grad into the immediately preceeding grad compute kernel. This is inconvenient to do today, because the grad accumulation happens separately from the custom autograd function, so you have to play tricks like https://github.com/deepseek-ai/TileKernels/blob/36d9e45d38e204ebb87e6f6e833821eee0482fe5/tile_kernels/modeling/mhc/ops/norm_fn.py#L167-L170 where you side channel whether or not the grad buffer has been allocated, then have your kernels do something different if there is an existing grad buffer (and have them return None to impede the normal grad acc codepath). Autograd should have some idiomatic way of doing this that is cleaner.

Non compiled autograd suffers from the same problem, as it doesn't include grad acc. Compiled autograd doesn't have this problem in principle, but you still have to have a compiler capable of doing the grad acc fusion, which is tricky because of functionalization in the compiler.

issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Problem

TorchInductor stores generated Python modules and autotuning results as individual files. Compiling different models, shapes, and configurations can accumulate a large number of small cache entries.

On clusters where cache directories reside on shared filesystems such as GPFS or
Lustre, these entries can exhaust an inode quota before disk capacity is exhausted, making subsequent `torch.compile` runs fail during cache writes.

## Current cache layout

The content-addressed cache includes hash-prefix directories containing generated `.py` modules and `.best_config` autotuning records. A simplified layout is:

```text
TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR/
  22/
    c22<hash>.py
    <hash>.best_config
  2v/
    c2v<hash>.py
    <hash>.best_config
  fxgraph/
  aotautograd/
  locks/
  ...
```

Python source and autotune metadata are the proposed initial targets. Other cache classes have different consumers and should not be redesigned as part of this work.

## Why an inode quota can stop a cluster job

An inode/file-count quota limits filesystem objects independently of the byte quota. GPFS, for example, exposes separate block and inode limits.
[IBM quota documentation](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/storage-scale/5.2.3?topic=reference-mmsetquota-command).

Consider this illustrative allocation, not a measured workload:

| Resource | Usage | Quota |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Storage | 20 GiB | 1 TiB |
| Files/directories | 100,000 | 100,000 |

Even a tiny new `.best_config` record can fail to be created. The problem is not the record's size: no additional filesystem object is allowed. Cache-write errors can interrupt compilation, and unrelated job outputs under the same quota can also fail.

Multiple jobs or nodes sharing a user/project quota consume the same allowance.
Repeated cache deletion frees inodes but sacrifices reuse; smaller individual files do not solve the file-count limit.

## Proposed alternative

Would an opt-in SQLite backend for autotuning records and `PyCodeCache` source be
acceptable?

- Store autotune records directly as database entries.
- Store Python source in the database and materialize temporary files when loading,
  inspection, or worker interfaces require a path.
- Keep the filesystem backend as the default and leave native objects, FX-graph
  entries, AOTAutograd entries, and remote-cache storage unchanged.

Proposed usage:

```sh
export TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_BACKEND=sqlite
export TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/node-local/cache
export TMPDIR=/path/to/node-local/runtime  # Existing writable directory.
python train.py
```

## Scope and cluster limitations

This is an inode-efficient **node-local cache**, not a distributed SQLite service. A writable database shared across nodes on GPFS/Lustre is not proposed as supported.

For cross-job or multi-node reuse, stage a consistent shared snapshot into each node's writable local cache before starting workers. Automatic shared read-only lookup with local writes would be a separate feature.

Native and graph caches still use files, so total savings depend on the workload.
Temporary source files also consume inodes: `TMPDIR` must be outside the constrained shared location. Fully read-only compilation, eviction, and bounded live temporary inode usage are outside this initial proposal.

---

Draft PR: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196994
Related Triton issue: https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/issues/11778

As this issue is literally preventing me to properly use `torch.compile` in an inode constrained context, as a temporary solution I'm using this patch: https://github.com/julien-blanchon/pytorch-inductor-sqlite-patch

---

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

Debugging build failures in `torch.utils.cpp_extension` is difficult because most failures are caused by local setup mismatches, not PyTorch bugs:

Host nvcc version mismatches with torch.version.cuda.

C++ ABI mismatches (_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI set to 0 locally while PyTorch wheel was built with 1).

Missing or incompatible host compilers (gcc, clang, cl.exe).

Missing build drivers or toolchain utilities like ninja.

When these mismatches occur, compilation fails deep inside setuptools / ninja with hundreds of lines of template backtraces, or compiles cleanly but causes a Segmentation Fault at runtime.

Add a lightweight, public pre-flight diagnostic check in torch.build:

```python
import torch

status = torch.build.check_environment()
if not status.is_ready:
    print(status.report())
```
Expected behavior of torch.build.check_environment():

Probe host C++ compiler version and verify _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI parity against the pre-built PyTorch binaries.

Check nvcc / ROCm compiler availability and version alignment with the active driver/CUDA runtime.

Validate presence of ninja, cmake, and required build utilities.

Return a structured Status object that prints plain error/warning messages without throwing raw compiler backtraces.

issues.body:
Finding the right batch size is a manual binary-search process. Set it too high, and jobs crash mid-run with CUDA out of memory errors. Set it too conservatively, and VRAM is underutilized.

This gets messier when:

Switching between local GPUs and cloud instances with different memory limits.

Running multi-GPU setups where nodes don't have identical free VRAM.

Standard DataLoader and DistributedSampler split data uniformly across ranks, which leaves higher-VRAM cards underutilized or forces manual tuning per environment.

An opt-in helper utility in torch.utils.data (like auto_fit_loader or an adaptive BatchSampler) could query free memory via torch.cuda.mem_get_info() and scale the batch size to fit within a target memory budget.

```python
loader = auto_fit_loader(
dataset=my_dataset,
max_vram_fraction=0.85,
parallel=True,
collate_fn=custom_collate
)
```

Rough implementation workflow:

Look at total vs available VRAM on the target device via torch.cuda.mem_get_info().

Run a 1-step trial pass with batch_size=1 and track peak memory allocation via torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() to estimate memory per sample.

Yield batch sizes computed as floor(usable_vram_budget / sample_memory_estimate).

In distributed environments (parallel=True), calculate rank-local batch sizes so cards with more VRAM take a larger portion of the workload without crashing smaller cards.

A few edge cases to consider:

Variable Sequence Lengths: For NLP or audio where input shapes vary per batch, the 1-step footprint estimate might undershoot if a long sequence appears later. A safety margin parameter is necessary.

DDP Gradient AllReduce: In Distributed Data Parallel, uneven batch sizes across ranks require careful handling so synchronization step counts match or use gradient accumulation per rank.

Is this something the core team would be open to having as a higher-level utility inside torch.utils.data? Happy to assemble a small standalone Python prototype if the core concept aligns with PyTorch's roadmap.

issues.body:
# [RFC] Opt-in mode that makes backward execute in the order predicted by `get_current_graph_task_execution_order`

### Motivation

`saved_tensors_hooks` enables memory-reduction schemes where large saved tensors are replaced by small deltas at pack time and reconstructed at unpack time. When the reconstruction is sequential (state k is rebuilt from state k+1, as in chunked KV-cache training, reversible networks, and similar recompute-from-delta schemes), the unpack hook needs requests to arrive in an order compatible with the reconstruction chain.

Today, that order is unspecified (documented in #198016, discussed in #198014). Real workloads observe out-of-chain-order requests: in awslabs/keys_values#148, a 36-layer / 1500-chunk training run received a request for chunk 1493 before the deltas for chunks 1494 and 1495 had been requested. Library code can defend against this (awslabs/keys_values#149 does, by walking the chain and parking early-reconstructed states), but the defense costs extra copies and considerable complexity that every library implementing this pattern must reinvent.

### Current behavior

The engine already prefers reverse-forward order, but only opportunistically:

- `ReadyQueue` is a priority queue; among *ready* tasks, the one with the highest `sequence_nr` runs first (`CompareNodeTaskTime` in `torch/csrc/autograd/engine.h`).
- A node only becomes ready when all its input gradients have accumulated, so a lower-`sequence_nr` node can run while a higher one is still waiting. This is where chain-order violations come from.
- `sequence_nr` is thread-local (`aten/src/ATen/SequenceNumber.cpp`), so the preference is not globally meaningful for multi-threaded forward.
- Multi-device backward uses one queue per device, so cross-device order is concurrent by construction.

Meanwhile, `torch::autograd::get_current_graph_task_execution_order()` (exposed for checkpoint debugging, requires `set_multithreading_enabled(False)`) already computes a full deterministic schedule: dependency-respecting, preferring higher `sequence_nr`, via a heap over the dependency counts.

### Proposal

An opt-in mode, e.g.

```python
with torch.autograd.set_deterministic_execution_order(True):
    loss.backward()
```

with the following contract:

1. Only valid with `set_multithreading_enabled(False)` and a single-device graph (error otherwise, at least initially).
2. The engine executes nodes in exactly the order `get_current_graph_task_execution_order()` returns, rather than popping the ready queue opportunistically. By construction that order respects dependencies, so no deadlock is possible; the change is to *wait* for the scheduled next node instead of running whatever is ready.
3. Consequence for `saved_tensors_hooks`: unpack requests arrive in a deterministic, documented order (the predicted schedule), which for single-threaded forward corresponds to reverse forward execution where dependencies allow.

This does not change the default. The default engine behavior and the "ordering is unspecified" contract from #198016 stay as they are.

### Known costs and open questions

- Precomputing the schedule requires an upfront graph traversal. `compute_dependencies` already traverses the graph, so the extra cost is one heap-ordered pass; acceptable for an opt-in mode, but worth measuring.
- In strict order, the engine may idle where it previously did useful work on another branch. For the target workloads (memory-bound, single device) this is an acceptable trade; numbers to be provided with the PR.
- Reentrant backward and recompute-in-backward (e.g. `torch.utils.checkpoint`) create nodes during execution that are not in the precomputed schedule. Options: (a) forbid in strict mode, (b) treat the recomputed subgraph as a nested strict schedule. Input welcome.
- `sequence_nr` collisions from multi-threaded forward make the schedule ill-defined; hence restriction 1.

### Alternatives considered

- Documenting the status quo — done in #198016; it clarifies but does not help sequential-reconstruction hooks.
- Defensive library code — works (awslabs/keys_values#149) but duplicates effort and memory in every library with this pattern.
- Prefetching all saved tensors for a region before backward — defeats the purpose of memory-reduction hooks.

I am happy to implement this behind the flag, with benchmarks, if the approach (or an amended one) is acceptable to the autograd maintainers.


cc @ezyang @albanD @gqchen @nikitaved @soulitzer @Varal7 @bobrenjc93
issues.title: [RFC] Opt-in mode that makes backward execute in the order predicted by get_current_graph_task_execution_order

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

`context_parallel()` does not support Gated DeltaNet.

It only intercepts SDPA and FlexAttention. Hybrid models such as Qwen3.5 mix those full-attention layers with GDN. GDN is a recurrence along time, so the Ring-style KV rotation used for SDPA cannot run it. GDN layers therefore cannot enter the same `context_parallel()` context, and sequence-sharded training of this architecture is blocked.

### Alternatives

Shard only the SDPA layers and leave GDN unsharded. GDN activations then stay full-sequence on every rank, which will have lower efficiency in memory and time.

### Additional context

Follow-up of #197487, now targeting `main`.

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

This is an RFC tracking issue for a zero-GC, 64-byte cache-line aligned contiguous flat arena allocator tailored for candidate token tree verification in speculative decoding.

* RFC Pull Request: https://github.com/pytorch/rfcs/pull/110
* Discourse Discussion: https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/rfc-0036-zero-gc-64-byte-cache-aligned-flat-arena-for-speculative-decoding-verification/3441

### Problem & Motivation
Speculative decoding verification on autoregressive LLMs generates high-frequency, short-lived token candidate trees. Standard dynamic tensor allocations during candidate branch verification introduce heap churn, memory fragmentation, and GC/synchronization overhead across multi-head verifiers.

### Pitch
By utilizing a flat 64-byte cache-line aligned arena, candidate token trees achieve CPU L1/L2 cache residency, eliminating per-step allocator locks and GC pressure, providing up to 1.83x lower p99 verification latency.


### Alternatives

Standard dynamic allocation via c10 default allocator, or generic out-of-tree pooling extensions that do not guarantee 64-byte L1 cache-line boundary alignment.


### Additional context

We welcome architectural review and feedback from the inference, memory allocator (c10), and performance SIG maintainers regarding integration boundaries.

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

I opened C++ PRs for a few losses (`#198226`, `#198341`, `#198413`, `#198370`) before there was an issue. Those were closed, correctly, because a new op needs an issue that a maintainer has marked actionable. This issue is that discussion. I am not asking anyone to re-open the PRs, and I will not send a new one until an issue is marked actionable.

The ops are all `CompositeImplicitAutograd`. None of them needs a new kernel. Each one is a reduction people currently reimplement, and the reimplementations disagree on the denominator and on what happens at 0.

1. **SMAPE.** `mean( |x - y| / max(eps, (|x| + |y|) / 2) )`. `eps` defaults to `1e-8`. Without the floor, a pair of zeros is `0/0`.
2. **Squared hinge.** `mean(relu(1 - y * x)^2)` with `y` in `{-1, +1}`. This is not `margin_ranking_loss` and not `hinge_embedding_loss`: both of those reduce a different expression.
3. **Focal loss**, multiclass, `mean(-alpha * (1 - pt)^gamma * log(pt))` where `pt = softmax(x)[y]`. Defaults `alpha=0.25`, `gamma=2`. Input `[N, C]`, target `[N]` int64. This is the classification form, not the detection form with a separate box loss.
4. **Poly-1 cross entropy.** `mean(CE + epsilon * (1 - pt))`, same `pt`. `epsilon=0` is ordinary cross entropy. Default `epsilon=1` matches the PolyLoss paper's first-order term.
5. **Dice.** Per-example `1 - (2 * sum(x * y) + eps) / (sum(x) + sum(y) + eps)`, then reduced over the batch. `x` and `y` are the same shape with a leading batch dimension. `eps` defaults to `1e-6`.

I would rather add one or two of these than all five. Focal and poly-1 are the ones I actually want, because both are a cross entropy plus a term in `pt`, and writing that on top of `cross_entropy` either drops the `pt` gradient or recomputes the softmax. SMAPE and squared hinge are small and have no close equivalent. Dice is the one I am least sure belongs in core: it is a segmentation loss, and most users want it per-channel with a squared denominator, which this version does not do.

### Alternatives

Leave them in user code. That is a reasonable answer for dice, and maybe for squared hinge. It is a worse answer for focal and poly-1, because the numerically stable path is the log-softmax that `cross_entropy` already has, and a second softmax to form `(1 - pt)^gamma` does not match that path.

`torch.nn.functional` wrappers would have the same compatibility constraint as a new native function: they cannot call the new op from existing Python until the FC window passes. If an op is accepted, the C++ change and the Python tests should land separately, two weeks apart.

### Additional context

I can put the formulas above against a short Python reference (a few dozen lines, values I have already checked locally) on whichever subset is marked actionable. I do not have a preference about the namespace (`torch.nn.functional` versus `torch.special`).

> An AI coding assistant helped me draft the earlier pull requests and the formulas in this issue. I checked each formula against the reduction I want, and I am dropping dice's per-channel and squared-denominator variants on purpose rather than guessing at them.

issues.body:
Ran into this again last week — spun up a run on a rented A100, model loaded fine, made it about 40 steps in and OOM'd. Would've been nice to know that before burning ~15 min of GPU time.

As far as I can tell there's no way to ask ahead of time "will this fit" — memory_allocated() and memory_reserved() only tell you what's already happened, not what's about to happen. So you just... run it and find out.

Not just me apparently, there's a package on PyPI (torch-kitsune) that exists purely to do this prediction outside of torch, and I found a 2025 paper (VeritasEst) doing basically the same thing with static/CPU analysis. Feels like something that should just live in core.

Rough idea for the API:

estimate = torch.cuda.estimate_memory(model, sample_input, optimizer=optimizer)

estimate.total_mb
estimate.fits(device=0)   # bool

with a breakdown available too (params_mb, optimizer_mb, activations_mb) in case you want to know what's actually eating the memory.

Params and optimizer state are easy to get exactly right — just sum sizes, apply the known multiplier per optimizer type (Adam ~2x, etc). Activations are the annoying part. My best idea is running the forward pass on meta tensors to get shapes without actually allocating anything, but that's going to fall over on data-dependent control flow or custom ops that don't support meta. So probably has to ship as "our best estimate" rather than something exact — worth saying that up front so nobody's surprised later.

Two things I'd want opinions on before going further:

should this live under torch.cuda, or somewhere backend-agnostic since the idea isn't CUDA-specific
is it worth doing activations at all in a first version, or ship params+optimizer only and add activations once people are actually using it

Not trying to solve batch-size auto-tuning or checkpointing here, just the "will this OOM" question.

cc @ptrblck @msaroufim @eqy @tinglvv @nWEIdia
issues.title: RFC: torch.cuda.estimate_memory

issues.body:
PyTorch publishes nightly wheels at https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly. This contains all the artifacts that are installed when PyTorch is built but leaves out everything else in the `build/` tree. This behavior is generally desirable.

However, some artifacts that are produced in the build tree can be useful for other purposes. For example, since enabling BOLT optimization for PyTorch, we keep the unoptimized libraries at `build/lib/prebolt`. These libraries can be used to profile PyTorch and generate profile data to be used for BOLT optimization.

Currently that data is generated using NVIDIA's internal builds since we need prebolt binaries for profiling. The ability to use builds from the PyTorch CI will help us generate better BOLT profile data and eventually help in profiling within PyTorch CI itself.

These binaries can also be helpful when trying to investigate performance regressions as pre-bolt binaries are not affected by staleness of the BOLT profile data.

I would like to request some way of downloading those pre-bolt artifacts. To avoid increasing load on PyTorch infra, we can have a short retention period for those libraries.

Related-to: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/188602

issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Motivation
Whole-model AOTInductor is the preferred path when it works, but a single unsupported construct anywhere in a model blocks the entire export. For a large class of real models the expensive compute is concentrated in a few submodules that are AOTI-compatible, while the blocker lives elsewhere.

Recommendation models are the clearest case. A torchrec DLRM-style model is structurally three dense blocks (dense_arch, inter_arch, over_arch) wrapped around a sparse embedding path. The dense blocks are plain MLPs and interaction arithmetic — exactly what Inductor is good at. The sparse path is not something you want to put through whole-model export. Today that means the dense compute gets nothing from AOTI, even though it is where the FLOPs are.

### Proposal
Regional AOTI compiles explicitly user-selected regions with AOTInductor while the surrounding model keeps running in eager Python. It is an incremental adoption path, not a replacement for whole-model AOTI.

```
from torch._inductor import regional_aoti

model = DLRM_DCN(...).eval()

# Mark the dense blocks; the sparse/embedding path stays eager.
regional_aoti.mark_region(model.dense_arch)
regional_aoti.mark_region(model.inter_arch)
regional_aoti.mark_region(model.over_arch)

result = regional_aoti.compile_regions(
    model, (dense_features, sparse_features),
    package_path="dlrm_regions.pt2dir",
)
print(result.report())
model = result.model
```

Serving reconstructs from eager weights plus the package:
```
model = DLRM_DCN(...).eval()
model.load_state_dict(torch.load("weights.pt", weights_only=True))
model = regional_aoti.load_regions(model, "dlrm_regions.pt2dir").model
logits = model(dense_features, sparse_features)
```

The user marks module instances (or annotates module classes), then calls compile_regions with representative inputs. Each selected region is functionalized, exported independently with non-strict Export, compiled to a PT2 artifact, validated against eager, and installed behind a Python wrapper. API surface is `mark_region`, `compile_regions`, `load_regions`, `replay_region`, `RegionConfig`.

**The central guarantee: the eager model remains the only owner of parameters and buffers.** Before Export, functional_call lifts state into explicit tensor inputs, and the wrapper re-gathers current state from the eager module on every invocation in a stable ABI order recorded in the manifest. For a recommendation model this is the property that makes the feature usable at all — embedding tables and dense weights keep living in the eager model, so normal checkpoint operations keep working:
```
model.load_state_dict(new_checkpoint)   # affects compiled regions immediately,
                                        # no recompile, no extra step
```

Consequences:

- state_dict() keys are identical before and after compilation
- tied parameters keep their aliasing; alias groups are recorded in the manifest
- mutating a parameter or buffer inside forward is rejected (state replacement between calls is fine)

Because of this, Regional AOTI reuses AOTI's execution path unchanged (Python loader, boxed_run, pytree flattening, tensor-only ABI) and uses none of its state-management path (load_constants, update_constant_buffer, swap_constant_buffer) — functionalization removes the artifact-owned copy those APIs exist to mutate. No changes to the AOTI C++ runtime are required.

### Other deliberate contract choices:
- Separate, explicit failure policies for compilation, package load, and runtime, so an onboarding setting can't silently become a production error-masking policy. Under compile_failure_policy=ERROR, install and publication are transactional: every region is attempted, but if any fails one aggregate error carries the full per-region report, the model is unchanged, and no package is published.
- No automatic runtime recompilation. A guard miss raises, or uses eager only if runtime fallback was explicitly enabled. No compiler in the serving path.
- Inference only, model.eval() required; export-time device/dtype/autocast state is part of the compatibility contract.
- A versioned, authoritative manifest. Filenames are never how a region is resolved, which keeps a future migration to a single multi-model PT2 archive a pure layout change.
- replay_region(bundle_dir) re-executes one failed stage from a reproduction bundle without the original model or inputs — so a PyTorch contributor who does not have your recommendation model can still reproduce your export failure.
- V1 rejects regions whose boundary or descendants have forward/backward module hooks, rather than silently dropping them.

Explicitly not in v1: training/backward, a Python-free hybrid runtime, automatic partitioning, multiple specializations per region, automatic runtime recompilation, CUDA Graph capture.

### More examples: partial success, dynamic shapes
**Partial success** — compile what works, leave the rest eager:
```
regional_aoti.mark_region(model.dense_arch)
regional_aoti.mark_region(model.sparse_arch)      # expected to fail export

result = regional_aoti.compile_regions(
    model, example_inputs, package_path="partial.pt2dir",
    compile_failure_policy=regional_aoti.FailurePolicy.EAGER,
)
print(result.report())
# dense_arch:  compiled
# sparse_arch: fallback at export
```

**Dynamic shapes** — serving batch size varies:
```
batch = torch.export.Dim("batch", min=1, max=4096)
regional_aoti.mark_region(
    model.dense_arch,
    config=regional_aoti.RegionConfig(dynamic_shapes={"features": {0: batch}}),
)
```

### Questions I'd most like comment on
- Which public models best represent this use case? DLRM-DCNv2 is my driving example, but I'd like non-recommendation cases too — HF / TIMM / TorchBench models where whole-model AOTI fails but a few expensive submodules are compatible. Most useful form: the model name, the construct that blocks whole-model export, and which submodule you would mark.
- Which compatibility checks must be hard errors, and which may permit opt-in eager fallback? My proposal: hard error for missing artifact, schema major-version mismatch, accelerator/device-type mismatch, state ABI mismatch, and dtype/rank/stride mismatch; hard error with opt-in fallback for a shape outside the declared dynamic range and for a non-tensor leaf differing from its specialized value. Which rows do you disagree with?

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Inductor template lookup builds its device key from the CUDA/HIP architecture name. A registered backend that does not have that field cannot use a lookup table. Keying the table with the driver product name is not a substitute: that string is not a stable architecture id, and once it is set the same rows are also considered for device-agnostic matches, including rows authored for CUDA.

A backend should be able to supply its own stable architecture id and have only rows for that id apply. Backends that do not supply one should stay out of lookup. CUDA and HIP behavior should stay as it is today.

Keeping lookup CUDA-only. Using the driver product name as the key.

A previous attempt is [#196414](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/196414). It was closed so this could be discussed on an issue first. I can update that approach once the issue is marked actionable.

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

`torch.vmap` raises for every `torch._foreach_*` op:

```python
import torch

x = torch.randn(4, 3)
torch.vmap(lambda t: torch.mul(t, 2))(x)  # works
torch.vmap(lambda t: torch._foreach_mul([t], 2)[0])(x)  # raises
```

```
RuntimeError: Batching rule not implemented for aten::_foreach_mul.Scalar. We could not generate a fallback.
```

The other `_foreach` ops that we tried fail the same way on 2.14.0 and on 2.16.0.dev20261007: `_foreach_add`, `_foreach_exp`, `_foreach_norm`, `_foreach_lerp`, and in-place forms such as `_foreach_add_` and `_foreach_mul_`. `vmap(grad(f))` also fails, while `grad(f)` without `vmap` works.

Expected: under `vmap`, a `_foreach` op gives the same result as the per-tensor op, `[torch.mul(t, 2) for t in tensors]`.

### Cause

The `_foreach` ops have no batching rules or decompositions, and the generic for-loop fallback rejects any op with a `Tensor[]` argument or return. `batchedTensorForLoopFallback` (`aten/src/ATen/functorch/BatchedFallback.cpp`) checks `areAllReturnsTensors(schema) && !areAnyArgumentsTensorList(schema)`.

Two possible directions:

- Register the per-tensor kernels (the `foreach_tensor_*_slow` functions in `ForeachOpsKernels.cpp`) for the `FuncTorchBatched` key, so that each tensor goes through the usual batching rules.
- Let the for-loop fallback slice and restack `Tensor[]` arguments and returns.

### Impact

The `_foreach_*` ops are private, but `torch.optim` (with `foreach=True`, the default on CUDA), `torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(foreach=True)` and libraries use them. In tensordict, `td * 2` failed inside `torch.vmap` (pytorch/tensordict#1923). pytorch/tensordict#2003 works around it with per-tensor ops when a `torch.func` transform is active.

issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

# RFC: Data-dependent loops in Inductor

**Status:** AI-assisted draft.  
**Reading time:** 5-10 minutes.

Prototype : https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/200743

## 1. Motivation

Inductor's existing Pointwise/Reduction model assumes that loop bounds are
uniform across iteration coordinates. A bound can be a dynamic shape symbol,
but it stays fixed as the enclosing loop advances.

Irregular, nonrectangular iteration spaces need that freedom. Jagged tensors,
jagged concatenation, sparse computations, grouped GEMM, and repeat_interleave
all involve work whose extent depends on data. We propose a general loop model
that describes all these applications through data-dependent bounds, using
ordinary tensors for data and metadata.

Let's start with the loop model. The examples are pseudocode.

## 2. How we view a data-dependent loop

### Bounds are functions; addresses are computations

Think of each bound as a function of the enclosing coordinates:

```python
for i in range(L0()):
    for j in range(L1(i)):
        for k in range(L2(i, j)):
            output[addr(i, j, k)] = compute(i, j, k)
```

Only coordinate arguments are shown. Bounds can read tensors, but return a
stable nonnegative integer for each enclosing coordinate tuple. Addresses can
contain nested reads too. Pointwise writes must map distinct valid coordinates
to distinct elements; collisions require scatter or reduction semantics.

### Apply this to jagged bias add

Take a matrix with row lengths `[3, 0, 2]`. Its five values and row boundaries
live in ordinary one-dimensional tensors. We broadcast `bias[b]` across row b:

```python
B = 3
values = tensor([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
offsets = tensor([0, 3, 3, 5])
bias = tensor([1, 10, 100])

# Jagged matrix:  [[10, 20, 30],
#                 [],
#                 [40, 50]]
# bias: [ 1
#         10
#         100]
# jagged-bias-add:[[11, 21, 31],
#                 [],
#                 [140, 150]]

N = values.numel()
datadep_output_flat_size = [N]  # [5]; offsets[-1] == 5
output = empty(datadep_output_flat_size)

def L(b):
    return offsets[b + 1] - offsets[b]

def addr(b, j):
    return offsets[b] + j

for b in range(B):
    for j in range(L(b)):
        output[addr(b, j)] = values[addr(b, j)] + bias[b]

# output = [11, 21, 31, 140, 150]
```

Two logical coordinates, `(b, j)`, select one physical address, `addr(b, j)`.
The bias stays constant within each row; the bound changes between rows.
The empty row performs no inner iterations.

### Keep the output shape separate

Materialization keeps an ordinary `[5]` buffer with stride `[1]`. Loads use
one physical index; logical consumers calculate `addr(b, j)`. Allocation
uses the known input shape.

## 3. Loop transformations on data-dependent loops

### Flattening: replace a loop nest with one loop

For a rectangular matrix with B rows and C columns, flattening is simple:

```python
for f in range(B * C):
    b, t = f // C, f % C
    output[f] = values[f] + bias[b]
```

Division and remainder recover the original coordinates because every row
has the same length.

For our jagged matrix, row boundaries vary. Flattening the packed values
looks like this:

```python
values = tensor([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
offsets = tensor([0, 3, 3, 5])
N = values.numel()  # 5

# Jagged view: [[10, 20, 30],
#               [],
#               [40, 50]]
#                    ^ f=4 -> b=2, t=1

for f in range(N):
    b = upper_bound(offsets, f) - 1  # f=4: 3 - 1 = 2
    t = f - offsets[b]              # f=4: 4 - 3 = 1
    output[f] = values[f] + bias[b]
```

`upper_bound` returns the index of the first offset strictly greater than f
(typically implemented with binary search on `offsets`).
Repeated offsets naturally skip empty rows.

### Parallelizing: assign independent work to workers

Flattening changes coordinates. Parallelizing decides which workers execute
iterations. A flattened loop can be parallelized, but we can also keep the
original nest:

```python
parallel for b in range(B):
    for j in range(L(b)):
        output[addr(b, j)] = values[addr(b, j)] + bias[b]
```

Workers have row `b`, so the inner loop needs no binary search. The initial GPU
schedule tiles this inner loop. Small B and uneven lengths can limit
parallelism; flattening may offer more parallel work.

Dense features provide additional parallel axes. Transformations must
preserve bound dependencies and reindex addresses.

### Vertical fusion: add, then sum

Now sum each row. Before fusion, the add and its
consumer traverse the domain separately:

```python
# Before: produce tmp[N], then consume it to produce result[B].
for b in range(B):
    for j in range(L(b)):
        tmp[addr(b, j)] = values[addr(b, j)] + bias[b]
for b in range(B):
    acc = 0
    for j in range(L(b)):
        acc += tmp[addr(b, j)]
    result[b] = acc

# After: one nest, with the add inside the reduction.
for b in range(B):
    acc = 0
    for j in range(L(b)):
        acc += values[addr(b, j)] + bias[b]
    result[b] = acc
```

The packed temporary disappears. Output sizes `[N]` and `[B]` differ, but
the computations share `(b, j)`.

### Horizontal fusion: two independent sums

Now consider sums of two jagged matrices sharing the same row boundaries:

```python
# Before: two independent reduction nests.
for b in range(B):
    a = 0
    for j in range(L(b)):
        a += left[addr(b, j)]
    left_sum[b] = a
for b in range(B):
    c = 0
    for j in range(L(b)):
        c += right[addr(b, j)]
    right_sum[b] = c

# After: one nest, with two accumulators.
for b in range(B):
    a, c = 0, 0
    for j in range(L(b)):
        a += left[addr(b, j)]
        c += right[addr(b, j)]
    left_sum[b], right_sum[b] = a, c
```

Vertical fusion requires matching producer/consumer addresses.

## 4. Triton code generation

Each Triton program can process several rows with different lengths. The bias-add
kernel follows our original nest:

```python
b = tl.program_id(0) * BBLOCK + tl.arange(0, BBLOCK)
bmask = b < B
start = tl.load(offsets + b, bmask, other=0)
end = tl.load(offsets + b + 1, bmask, other=0)
length = end - start
bias_value = tl.load(bias + b, bmask, other=0)

for jstart in tl.range(0, tl.max(tl.where(bmask, length, 0)), JBLOCK):
    j = jstart + tl.arange(0, JBLOCK)
    mask = bmask[:, None] & (j[None, :] < length[:, None])
    p = start[:, None] + j[None, :]
    value = tl.load(values + p, mask, other=0)
    tl.store(output + p, value + bias_value[:, None], mask)
```

Each Triton program iterates up to the maximum sequence length in its block,
using each row's own length for jagged masking of loads and stores.

## 5. Three further applications

Assume output offsets and allocation sizes are already available.

### 3D nested jagged format (CSF)

```python
for b in range(B):
    for j in range(row_offsets[b + 1] - row_offsets[b]):
        parent = row_offsets[b] + j
        for k in range(depth_offsets[parent + 1] - depth_offsets[parent]):
            p = depth_offsets[parent] + k
            output[p] = values[p] + bias[b]
```

In this Compressed Sparse Fiber (CSF) layout, the depth bound depends on both
row `b` and column `j`. The output is a packed vector.

### Slice jagged rows, then reduce

```python
for b in range(B):
    for j in range(take[b]):
        p = input_offsets[b] + starts[b] + j
        acc = 0
        for d in range(D):
            acc += values[p, d]
        output[output_offsets[b] + j] = acc
```

The slice need not be materialized. Output size is `[sum(take)]`; body
evaluations are `sum(take) * D`. Concatenation similarly uses a bound
`length_left[b] + length_right[b]` and selects the source.

### Pairwise products between two jagged feature sets

```python
for b in range(B):
    for j in range(J(b)):
        for k in range(K(b)):
            p, q = left_offsets[b] + j, right_offsets[b] + k
            acc = 0
            for d in range(D):
                acc += left[p, d] * right[q, d]
            output[output_offsets[b] + j * K(b) + k] = acc
```

Each batch produces a matrix of size `J(b) * K(b)`. Together they occupy
`[sum_b J(b) * K(b)]`. This expresses ragged batched matmul or similarity
scores using multiply and sum; tensor-core scheduling is further work.

## 6. Proposed IR

Reuse `ir.Pointwise` and `ir.Reduction`, keeping their logical ranges separate
from physical output metadata:

- `datadep_output_flat_size`: the actual output tensor size.
- `datadep_output_indexer`: the address function for surviving output coordinates.
- `datadep_iteration_numel`: optional work-count metadata, including reductions;
  unnecessary for this bias-add example.

`inner_fn` builds a graph over symbolic coordinates. Register the bound in
that graph while describing the same bias-add computation:

```python
J = ir.DataDependentRange("j")

def addr(b, j):
    return ops.load("offsets", b) + ops.index_expr(j, torch.int64)

def inner_fn(index):
    b, j = index
    length = ops.load("offsets", b + 1) - ops.load("offsets", b)
    ops.register_datadep_range(length, J)
    p = ops.indirect_indexing(addr(b, j), N, wrap_neg=False)
    return ops.load("values", p) + ops.load("bias", b)

pointwise = ir.Pointwise(
    device=device, dtype=dtype, inner_fn=inner_fn, ranges=[B, J],
    datadep_output_flat_size=[N],
    datadep_output_indexer=lambda index: addr(*index),
)
```

`J` names the bound; `j` is the coordinate. `register_datadep_range` records
that association and returns no value. Tracing uses symbolic coordinates;
generated execution evaluates the bound before entering J, including when J
is empty. Bound loads and
element loads are captured together, so their dependencies remain visible
without a separate bound callback. Operations sharing a range token must use
the same bound.

Reductions register bounds the same way and place reduced tokens in
`reduction_ranges`. The initial implementation targets CUDA/Triton. Frontend
recognition, output-size discovery, and general state-dependent while loops
are separate work.

## Appendix: prototype benchmarks

There is no frontend yet. We constructed `ir.Pointwise` and `ir.Reduction`
directly, assuming lowering had already produced them. We then used Inductor's
actual scheduler, fusion, and Triton code generation, and executed the generated
kernels against references. The suite covers 18 non-attention FBGEMM operations
and four PyTorch applications, with an additional BF16 grouped GEMM measurement.

### Setup and baselines

- PyTorch: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/200743
- NVIDIA H100; Triton 3.9.0.
- `B=128`, maximum jagged length 512, `D=128`. Seeded, shuffled lengths have
  mean 360, standard deviation 64.06, range 208-512, and `NNZ=46,080`.
- Feature tensors use packed `[NNZ, D]` or padded `[B, 512, D]` storage.
  Jagged2 cases contain `J(b) * J(b)` squares. Grouped GEMM varies
  `M=J(b)` with fixed `K=N=128`. CSR matrices are `[128, 512]` with mean
  row degree 360, approximately 70% density.
- FP32 inputs and outputs, with TF32 disabled. 

FBGEMM baselines retain the original Triton kernels from
[this commit](https://github.com/pytorch/FBGEMM/tree/31323796c75a308d4537cb4b0119f91fc4166c2b).
We searched bounded tile/warp configurations and enabled Inductor autotuning.
The extra applications use native PyTorch eager operations and their library
implementation choices, as identified in the table.

Our GEMMs use **multiply followed by sum**; Tensor Core/dot scheduling is still
future work. That fast path is about 11 times faster than our BF16 mul+sum implementation.

Times are median microseconds from CUDA events around the complete callable,
including required padding fills and returned offsets. Input setup, compilation,
and tuning are excluded. **Speedup = baseline / IR time**; below 1 means slower.
Kernel counts refer to our emitted Triton definitions. 

### Results

| Operation | Dtype | Baseline | Baseline us | IR us | Speedup | IR kernels | Result |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Packed values add | FP32 | FBGEMM Triton | 36.74 | 38.14 | 0.963x | 1 | Pass |
| Dense vector x jagged matrix | FP32 | FBGEMM Triton | 71.52 | 23.17 | 3.087x | 1 | Pass |
| Jagged to dense, general | FP32 | FBGEMM Triton | 40.22 | 31.87 | 1.262x | 1 | Pass |
| Jagged to dense, optimized 2D | FP32 | FBGEMM Triton | 33.18 | 31.46 | 1.055x | 1 | Pass |
| Dense to jagged | FP32 | FBGEMM Triton | 30.24 | 33.28 | 0.909x | 1 | Pass |
| Dense prefix + jagged concat | FP32 | FBGEMM Triton | 12.48 | 7.17 | 1.741x | 2 | Pass |
| Jagged2 to padded dense | FP32 | FBGEMM Triton | 132.99 | 98.02 | 1.357x | 1 | Pass |

| Jagged x dense BMM | FP32 | FBGEMM Triton | 67.14 | 557.41 | 0.120x | 1 | Pass |
| Jagged x jagged BMM, dense output | FP32 | FBGEMM Triton | 61.44 | 872.54 | 0.070x | 1 | Pass |
| Array x jagged BMM | FP32 | FBGEMM Triton | 165.58 | 2153.26 | 0.077x | 1 | Pass |
| Jagged x jagged BMM, packed output | FP32 | FBGEMM Triton | 197.70 | 29703.01 | 0.007x | 1 | Pass |

issues.body:
## Summary

`rerun-disabled-tests` (`PYTORCH_TEST_RERUN_DISABLED_TESTS=1`) reruns tests that are still skipped by a DISABLED GitHub issue, so a run of greens can justify closing that issue. This RFC adds the same kind of signal for a code skip: a skip for a known failure on a machine that can run the test. A capability skip stays skipped. That is a missing library, `onlyCUDA`, `skipIf` / `skipUnless`, `requires_*`, or a version floor.

Two drafts start this work:

- PyTorch, which publishes the signal and does not delete decorators: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199916
- test-infra, which would later open one daily draft proposing deletions and does not merge them: https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026

## Motivation

| Who | Need |
| --- | --- |
| Test authors | A skip for a known failure can outlive the failure. With no GitHub issue to close, nothing prompts deleting the decorator. |
| CI | The nightly job already reruns DISABLED-issue skips. A code skip never produces a pass or a fail. |

## Background

A DISABLED issue skip already has a loop. While the issue is open, the nightly job runs the test. 150 greens in 7 days and 0 reds, plus 14 quiet days, are the bar for closing the issue. Closing it removes the skip.

A code skip has no issue. The decorator is the only record, and it stays in force during `rerun-disabled-tests`. The nightly job cannot tell a fixed code skip from one that still fails.

This RFC leaves the issue path and the `rerun_disabled_tests` upload unchanged. Code-skip reruns go to a separate prefix, `rerun_disabled_code_skips`.

```
Python skip decorator
        ↓
mark safe-to-rerun skips
        ↓
pytest collection temporarily removes those skips
        ↓
test body passes, fails, or remains skipped
        ↓
JUnit XML retains the original skip reason
        ↓
results upload to rerun_disabled_code_skips
        ↓
test-infra can eventually propose deleting fixed decorators
```

Only code skips are marked safe to rerun. Capability skips are not marked.

Collection drops those marks for that job only. The decorator stays in the source file.

The body then passes, fails, or remains skipped. It remains skipped when a capability skip still applies. A pass or a fail does not edit the file.

The JUnit row keeps the original skip reason, so a pass or a fail can still be matched to the decorator that was lifted.

Those rows upload to `rerun_disabled_code_skips` and are not added to `rerun_disabled_tests`.

test-infra can later propose deleting decorators that clear the same bar as closing a DISABLED issue: 150 greens in 7 days and 0 reds. There is no 14-day quiet period, because a code skip has no issue. https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026 is that last step. It would open one daily draft pull request. That draft does not merge.

## Goals

- Run code skips in `rerun-disabled-tests`.
- Leave capability skips skipped, on every platform.
- Keep the original skip reason on the result when the body passes or fails.
- Upload code-skip reruns only to `rerun_disabled_code_skips`.
- Leave `rerun_disabled_tests` unchanged.
- Propose decorator deletions in a later human-reviewed draft. Do not delete them here.

## Non-goals

- Deleting decorators in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199916.
- Merging a deletion from https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026.
- Rerunning capability skips.
- Changing the DISABLED-issue path, its upload, or its 14 quiet days.
- Limiting the split to one platform.

## Alternatives

- Leave code skips until someone deletes them by hand. A fixed test stays skipped, with no green-run count behind a deletion.
- Upload code-skip reruns into `rerun_disabled_tests`. This RFC uses a separate prefix so the existing collection stays as it is.
- Rerun every skip. Failures on a machine that cannot run the test would be mixed in with real regressions.

## Additional context

- PyTorch: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/199916
- test-infra: https://github.com/pytorch/test-infra/pull/9026
- Deletion bar: 150 greens in 7 days and 0 reds. No 14-day quiet period.

Authored with assistance from Cursor.


cc @malfet @pytorch/pytorch-dev-infra @mruberry
issues.title: [RFC] Rerun code skips in rerun-disabled-tests

issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Downstream PyTorch builds need to support deployment environments with
an existing accelerator software stack while reusing the upstream Linux
wheel build process as much as possible. Upstream support for
customization would reduce downstream maintenance and build divergence,
while allowing downstream builds to benefit from ongoing improvements
to the shared build process.

Examples from Alibaba downstream requirements include:
1. Cloud images where the accelerator SDK and PyTorch are installed and
 managed separately.
2. Bare-metal deployments with an existing accelerator SDK installation.
3. Hardware-vendor distributions that need to select which runtime
 libraries are included in downstream PyTorch wheels.

These environments may provide an accelerator software stack outside
the Python environment. A distributor may still choose to bundle
selected dependencies in its PyTorch wheels, such as MPI or OpenMP
libraries, depending on deployment requirements.

We would like upstream to provide a way to customize downstream Linux
wheels while retaining the existing behavior for official builds. The
required customization includes selecting which shared libraries are
bundled, supporting runtime libraries supplied by the deployment
environment, and ensuring that dependency metadata and platform tags
accurately describe the resulting wheel.

This request concerns downstream-built artifacts. We are not requesting
an additional official wheel variant or asking upstream to validate
arbitrary downstream runtime combinations.
Downstream distributors would remain responsible for testing and
supporting their artifacts, including compatibility with the accelerator
software stacks in our deployment environments.


### Alternatives

I have considered:
1. Installing with --no-deps: This skips Python dependency installation,
but does not customize bundled libraries, ELF search paths, or the
wheel's declared dependency metadata.
2. Maintaining a separate build pipeline or patching the upstream
scripts: This provides flexibility but requires ongoing synchronization
with upstream packaging changes.
3. Repackaging completed wheels downstream: This still requires tracking
upstream packaging details and modifying metadata and ELF dependencies
after the build.

### Additional context

A prototype currently consists of five commits covering dependency
handling, runtime paths, platform tagging, and build configuration
overrides.
It is available as a basis for discussion, and its interface and scope
can be revised based on maintainer feedback.
We would appreciate feedback from the binaries and release-engineering
maintainers on whether this is an appropriate capability and what
customization boundary would be maintainable.

cc @malfet @atalman @tinglvv @nWEIdia
issues.title: [CD] Support customization of downstream Linux wheel builds

issues.body:
This issue tracks every deprecation, frozen component, and pending removal in PyTorch. Each one has its own tracking issue, listed as a sub-issue below, so progress is visible at a glance.

### Process

This follows the [backward compatibility policy](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/wiki/PyTorch%27s-Python-Frontend-Backward-and-Forward-Compatibility-Policy), which is the source of truth for warning periods.

1. **Deprecate in release N.** Warn on use. The warning names the start version, the removal version, and the tracking issue, e.g. ``"`torch.foo` is deprecated since 2.15 and will be removed in 2.17. Use `torch.bar` instead. See https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/NNNN"``.
2. **Warn for at least two releases** (180 days for nightly users). The earliest removal is N+2.
3. **Remove** in N+2 or later, and close the tracking issue.

Frozen components (no new features, bugs closed as won't-fix) are tracked the same way, with removal target `none` until a removal is planned.

### Adding an entry

1. File a tracking issue with the [Deprecation tracking](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/new?template=deprecation.yml) form. It is labeled `module: deprecation`.
2. Attach it as a sub-issue of this issue.
3. Keep its `Next step` field current (e.g. `remove in 2.17`). Milestones are assigned from it at each branch cut, following the convention that milestone X means "land right after the X branch cut".

Agents follow the same steps through the `deprecate-feature` skill (#201299).

### Related

- #55953: previous deprecation tracker (closed)
- #49642: turn deprecation warnings into errors in CI
- #60149: find out when an API was added or changed

issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

In signal processing, time-series analysis, audio/speech modeling (`torchaudio`), and mathematical morphology, sliding window extrema (rolling min and max) over 1D sequences are fundamental operations:
1. **Audio & Speech**: Dynamic range compression (DRC), temporal envelope extraction, and energy tracking across large acoustic windows ($K = 128 \dots 4096$).
2. **Signal & Financial Time-Series**: Rolling volatility, rolling Sharpe, min-max normalization, local peak detection, and trend tracking.
3. **Computer Vision & Morphology**: Morphological dilation and erosion with 1D flat structuring elements.

#### Current Limitations in PyTorch:
1. **`torch.nn.functional.max_pool1d`**:
   - Only supports max, not min (there is no `min_pool1d` in PyTorch).
   - Constrained input rank: crashes on 1D tensors `(L)` and 4D+ tensors `(..., L)` with `Expected 2D or 3D tensor`.
   - Constrained padding: strictly raises `ValueError` if `padding > kernel_size // 2`.
   - Complexity: Executes a brute-force nested loop over $K$, requiring $O(K \cdot N)$ comparisons. For large window sizes ($K \ge 500$), this becomes a major bottleneck.
2. **`tensor.unfold(dim, size, step).max(dim=-1)`**:
   - Materializes overlapping windows of shape `(..., L_out, K)`, incurring $O(K \cdot N)$ memory overhead. For sequences of length $L = 10^6$ and $K = 5,000$, this causes CUDA OOM.
3. **Custom Python / Loops**:
   - Unacceptably slow on large datasets and breaks TorchScript / Dynamo integration.

#### Proposed Feature:
Add `sliding_window_max` and `sliding_window_min` to `torch.nn.functional` (and re-export under `torch.signal`):

```python
torch.nn.functional.sliding_window_max(
    input: Tensor,
    kernel_size: int,
    stride: int = 1,
    padding: int = 0,
    return_indices: bool = False
) -> Union[Tensor, tuple[Tensor, Tensor]]

torch.nn.functional.sliding_window_min(
    input: Tensor,
    kernel_size: int,
    stride: int = 1,
    padding: int = 0,
    return_indices: bool = False
) -> Union[Tensor, tuple[Tensor, Tensor]]
```

### Alternatives

1. **`torch.nn.functional.max_pool1d`**:
   - Pros: Built-in, fast for small $K \in [2, 7]$.
   - Cons: No min-pooling support, rejects 1D inputs, rejects `padding > kernel_size // 2`, scales as $O(K \cdot N)$.
2. **`x.unfold(-1, kernel_size, stride).max(-1)`**:
   - Pros: Supports any dimension.
   - Cons: High memory bloat ($K \times$ memory multiplier), causing CUDA OOM on long sequences.
3. **`scipy.ndimage.maximum_filter1d` / `scipy.signal`**:
   - Pros: Available in SciPy.
   - Cons: Requires roundtripping to NumPy/CPU, breaks CUDA pipelines and autograd backpropagation.

### Additional context

#### Benchmarks:
Comparing Monotonic Deque ($O(N)$ comparisons) against `unfold() + max()` ($O(N \cdot K)$) on sequence length $L = 10^6$:

| Window Size $K$ | Monotonic Deque ($O(N)$) | Unfold ($O(N \cdot K)$) | Memory Savings |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| $K = 50$ | 12.1 ms | 38.4 ms | **98% less RAM** |
| $K = 500$ | 12.4 ms | 284.1 ms | **99.8% less RAM** |
| $K = 5,000$ | 12.5 ms | **CUDA OOM** | **Eliminates OOM** |

A reference implementation with full test coverage and gradient verification is prepared and ready for review.


cc @mikaylagawarecki
issues.title: [Feature Request] Native 1D sliding window extrema (min/max) for torch.signal / torch.nn.functional

issues.body:
- **Author(s)**: Fujun Han (@Peter9606)
- **Status**: Draft
- **Related Issues / PRs**: [#190875](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/190875), [#201039](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201039)
- **AI Assistance**: Drafted with Cursor. Reviewed and edited before posting.

---

## Summary

[#190875](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/190875) added FlyDSL to Inductor as an optional DSL path next to CuteDSL and CUTLASS: `FlyDSLTemplate`, `FlyDSLScheduling`, async compile, autotune, and an in-tree GEMM template for AMD `gfx950`.

[#201039](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201039) tried to drop the `torch.version.hip` check from the shared `runtime_available()` gate. Review (@jgong5) asked to settle the out-of-tree model before more code:

1. How does a non-ROCm `PrivateUse1` device with its own FlyDSL compile backend enter Inductor?
2. Does that path still depend on the `"cuda"` device tag or `torch.backends.cuda.is_built()`?
3. How does it reuse the existing FlyDSL scaffolding without monkey-patching `mm.py` globals?

This RFC answers those three. Shared helpers only ask whether the `flydsl` package is usable. Templates, capability checks, and autotune configs register per `(device_type, family)`. gfx950 stays the in-tree default. Third-party kernels stay out of `pytorch/pytorch`.

The registration API is experimental/internal. It is for out-of-tree device plugins, not a stable user-facing ABI.

---

## Motivation

@jgong5 asked to settle design before more code. The current tree maps onto that request as follows.

| Concern | Current code |
|------|------|
| Third-party devices use `PrivateUse1`; FlyDSL routing checks `"cuda"` | FlyDSL template buffers are dispatched by `CUDACombinedScheduling`, which is registered for the `"cuda"` tag. ROCm works because it uses that tag too. |
| FlyDSL should not be coupled to the CUDA device tag | `runtime_available()` still starts with `_cuda.is_built()`. A PrivateUse1-only build never passes. |
| In-tree code is ROCm/gfx950; monkey-patching is not an official hook | `mm.py` holds a single global `flydsl_mm_template` and gfx950-shaped kwargs. A third party that needs a different Jinja template or config set has to overwrite those globals. |

[#201039](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201039) only removes the `hip is None` early return. gfx950 behavior on the current call path stays the same. It does not fix the three rows above.

Some out-of-tree backends also present CUDA-facade tensors (`device.type == "cuda"`) while registering a PrivateUse1 name. Lookup by the renamed backend name then misses the provider. Device identity is specified in the next section so that case is not implicit.

### What this RFC reuses

Third-party integration has two layers. This RFC only constrains the second.

1. **FlyDSL package** (`flydsl`): DSL, JIT, compile backend. Vendors implement `FLYDSL_COMPILE_BACKEND=<target>` inside that package. They do not pretend to be `gfx*` in PyTorch.
2. **Inductor FlyDSL scaffolding** (`torch/_inductor/codegen/flydsl`): `FlyDSLTemplate`, `FlyDSLTemplateBuffer`, `FlyDSLScheduling`, `async_compile.flydsl`, `FlyDSLBenchmarkRequest`, autotune. Vendor differences belong in which device registers which template and configs.

---

## Device identity

Provider lookup uses `layout.device.type` as Inductor sees it during lowering. That is the name Dynamo/Inductor already use for `register_backend_for_device`.

**Preferred:** a real PrivateUse1 device. `rename_privateuse1_backend("custom_device")` so tensors are `custom_device`, Inductor scheduling is registered for `"custom_device"`, and FlyDSL templates register under `"custom_device"`. gfx950 (`("cuda", "mm")`) is never queried.

**Compatibility, fail closed:** some plugins still expose CUDA-facade tensors, so `layout.device.type == "cuda"`. Those plugins register under `"cuda"` (the type lowering actually observes) and `enabled()` must return false on real CUDA and ROCm. The in-tree gfx950 entry keeps `torch.version.hip` plus `gfx950`. Two `"cuda"` entries may coexist; isolation is the `enabled()` predicate, not the registry key.

**Rejected:** register under `"custom_device"` while tensors still report `"cuda"`. Lowering would look up `("cuda", "mm")` and either take gfx950 or take nothing.

Subclassing `CUDACombinedScheduling` is not required and is not the recommended hook. That class is the `"cuda"` tag coupling this RFC is removing for PrivateUse1.

---

## Proposal

Shared code asks two questions: is the FlyDSL runtime importable, and does this device have a registered template whose `enabled()` is true. Arch, dtype, and kernel ABI stay in that template's callables. HIP and `"cuda"` are not FlyDSL admission checks.

### 1. Shared runtime gate

`runtime_available()` in `torch/_inductor/codegen/flydsl/flydsl_utils.py` only checks the package:

- `flydsl` is importable
- `flydsl._mlir` is present
- version is in the pinned range (currently `0.3.x`)

It does not check `torch.version.hip` or `torch.backends.cuda.is_built()`. `_cuda.is_built()` may still appear on CUDA/ROCm's own paths. Leaving it in the shared FlyDSL gate blocks a legal PrivateUse1-only build.

Device capability is `enabled(layout)`. Whether the device is wired into Inductor at all is `register_backend_for_device`.

### 2. Scheduling: hold `FlyDSLScheduling`, do not inherit `"cuda"`

This RFC does not change `register_backend_for_device`. A PrivateUse1 backend registers its device name and its full Inductor backend (scheduling plus wrapper codegen):

```python
from torch._inductor.codegen.common import register_backend_for_device

register_backend_for_device(
    "custom_device",
    device_scheduling=CustomDeviceCombinedScheduling,
    device_wrapper_codegen=CustomDeviceWrapperCodegen,
)
```

`register_backend_for_device` is the Inductor backend entry. It is not a FlyDSL on-switch. Wrapper codegen, compile workers, and cache paths still have to handle that device. The template registry only supplies FlyDSL candidates.

The backend's combined scheduling holds a `FlyDSLScheduling` and delegates `FlyDSLTemplateBuffer` nodes to it. That is the FlyDSL slice of `CUDACombinedScheduling.choose_node_backend`, not a copy of CUTLASS / CK / CuteDSL / NVGEMM routing. A PrivateUse1 backend that already has Triton (or equivalent) adds this delegation; it does not subclass `CUDACombinedScheduling`.

```python
class CustomDeviceCombinedScheduling(BaseScheduling):
    def __init__(self, scheduler):
        super().__init__(scheduler)
        self._triton_scheduling = CustomDeviceTritonScheduling(scheduler)
        self._flydsl_scheduling = FlyDSLScheduling(scheduler)

    def choose_node_backend(self, node):
        if self._flydsl_scheduling.is_flydsl_template(node):
            return self._flydsl_scheduling
        return self._triton_scheduling
```

The supported install hook is `torch.<backend>._inductor_backend_init`, already called from `init_backend_registration`. That hook registers both the Inductor backend and the FlyDSL template.

### 3. Template registration (function, mm-only contract)

A working-tree follow-up to #201039 added `register_flydsl_gemm_arch`. That only opens the gfx950-shaped arch gate; plugins still overwrite `flydsl_mm_template` and `get_flydsl_mm_template_kwargs`. This registry **replaces** that arch set and those globals.

The first landing is GEMM (`family="mm"`). The registry is keyed by `(device_type, family)` so a later family can reuse the table without a second mechanism. This RFC does not define configs for anything except `mm`.

No provider ABC and no `FlyDSLMmContext`. Inductor already registers backends and lowerings as functions. The mm-only data is:

```python
def register_flydsl_template(
    device_type: str,
    family: str,
    *,
    name: str,
    template: FlyDSLTemplate,
    enabled: Callable[[Layout], bool],
    configs: Callable[..., list[dict[str, Any]]],
    replace: bool = False,
) -> None:
    ...
```

| Piece | Role |
|------|------|
| `name` | Registry identity. Must equal `template.name`. `FlyDSLTemplate` already rejects two templates with the same name and different source, so out-of-tree names stay distinct (`mm_flydsl` in-tree, `mm_flydsl_<backend>` out-of-tree). |
| `enabled(layout) -> bool` | Device, arch, dtype. Shape and kernel ABI do not belong here; `Layout` does not carry matmul strides, K alignment, or static M/N/K. |
| `template` | The `FlyDSLTemplate` instance. |
| `configs(layout, mat1, mat2, ...) -> list[dict]` | Autotune knobs only (tile, LDS, MMA, and the kernel's own ABI filters). Empty list means this shape does not participate. Do not put `input_nodes` or `layout` in the dicts; `mm.py` passes those at `maybe_append_choice`. |

Each `(device_type, family)` maps to a list. Registration appends. The same `name` under the same key raises unless `replace=True`, which replaces only that name. Registering one entry must not rewrite another device. Every entry whose `enabled()` is true may contribute autotune candidates.

### 4. Selection in `mm.py`

`mm.py` keeps operator-level gates. Each registered template keeps kernel ABI and configs.

| Stays in `mm.py` | Moves into the gfx950 (or third-party) `configs` / `enabled` |
|------|------|
| `max_autotune` / `_use_autotune_backend("FLYDSL")` | tile / LDS / MMA configs |
| static shape / nonzero | K alignment, dtypes that kernel accepts |
| runtime_available() | Jinja source |
| | HIP + gfx950 for the in-tree entry |

```python
def append_flydsl_mm_choices(
    choices,
    layout,
    mat1,
    mat2,
    *,
    static_shape,
    is_nonzero,
    input_nodes,
) -> None:
    if not (config.max_autotune or config.max_autotune_gemm):
        return
    if not _use_autotune_backend("FLYDSL"):
        return
    if not flydsl_utils.runtime_available():
        return
    if not static_shape or not is_nonzero:
        return

    for entry in flydsl_utils.get_flydsl_templates(layout.device.type, "mm"):
        if not entry.enabled(layout):
            continue
        for knobs in entry.configs(layout, mat1, mat2):
            entry.template.maybe_append_choice(
                choices,
                input_nodes=input_nodes,
                layout=layout,
                **knobs,
            )
```

The vendored gfx950 kernel becomes the default entry for `("cuda", "mm")`. Its `enabled()` keeps the current HIP and gfx950 checks, so ROCm behavior stays as in #190875.

`use_flydsl_gemm_template(layout)` can remain a convenience predicate: runtime available, and at least one `"mm"` entry for `layout.device.type` has `enabled(layout)` true.

### 5. Workers and cache

Choice generation and registry lookup run in the parent during lowering.

`async_compile.flydsl` workers receive generated source. They do not consult the registry. Autotune benchmark workers receive the compiled artifact / source the same way.

Fork inherits the module-level registry. Spawn does not. Spawned compile/autotune workers still do not need it if they only compile source the parent already generated. If a future path re-imports torch and re-lowers in a spawned process, that process must run the same `_inductor_backend_init`.

`FlyDSLTemplate.hash_key` is `name + source`. Unique `template.name` plus distinct source is the compile identity. Precompile and benchmark keys that currently hash the choice should keep `template.name` so two providers cannot reuse each other's results. `configs` must match the same capability the `enabled()` predicate claims.

Registration must complete before the parent lowers a graph. The install path is `_inductor_backend_init`, not an import side effect in the parent that spawn workers will never see.

---

## Alternatives

**Provider ABC plus `FlyDSLMmContext`.** Same data as the function hook, with a GEMM-typed context object on a family-generic registry. Heavier than `register_backend_for_device` / `register_lowering`. Rejected for this RFC. If a later family needs a richer object, it can add one without making GEMM the base class.

**`register_flydsl_gemm_arch` only.** Opens the arch gate and still requires monkey-patching the template and kwargs. Does not answer @jgong5. Replaced by this registry.

**CUDA-facade as the only supported model; subclass `CUDACombinedScheduling`.** Matches some current plugins. Couples FlyDSL to the `"cuda"` tag, which is what the #201039 review rejected. Kept only as a fail-closed compatibility path under `"cuda"`.

---

## Non-Goals

- Eager / `torch._native` overrides. Separate from Inductor templates.
- Template families other than `mm`. Later families may reuse the same registry.
- Third-party templates or hardware lowering in the PyTorch tree.
- Changing default gfx950 behavior or heuristics.
- Upstream CI on third-party hardware. Stub providers are the landing bar.
- FlyDSL compile-backend internals in PyTorch. Those stay in the `flydsl` package.
- A long-term ABI for random user code. This is an experimental plugin hook.

---

## Tests

Stub-only. No third-party plugin in CI.

- Register / `replace=True` / duplicate `name` without `replace` raises
- Two entries under one key: only those with `enabled()` true contribute
- Entry registered for `"custom_device"` is not selected when `layout.device.type == "cuda"`
- gfx950 `enabled()` is false without HIP / gfx950 (ROCm regression)
- CUDA-facade case: two entries under `"cuda"`, only the matching `enabled()` contributes
- Distinct `template.name` so `FlyDSLTemplate.all_templates` does not collide
- Stub `CombinedScheduling` forwards `FlyDSLTemplateBuffer` to `FlyDSLScheduling` without subclassing `CUDACombinedScheduling`
- Spawn worker compiles already-generated source without the registry

---

## Implementation plan

@jgong5 asked to settle this design before more code. [#201039](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/201039) waits on agreement here, then lands as PR 1.

1. **PR 1: Gate.** `runtime_available()` checks the FlyDSL package only. HIP / gfx950 stay in the in-tree GEMM predicate. This is #201039 after the comments match this RFC.
2. **PR 2: Registry and in-tree migration.** Add `register_flydsl_template`; move gfx950 into `("cuda", "mm")`; switch `mm.py` to the dispatch above; remove `register_flydsl_gemm_arch` and the `flydsl_mm_template` / `get_flydsl_mm_template_kwargs` globals. gfx950 numbers stay the same.
3. **PR 3: Tests and docs.** The stub list in the previous section, plus a short extension note. No third-party hardware in CI.

---

## Open questions

1. All `enabled()` entries contribute to autotune (proposed), versus first match wins. First-match would hide a second in-tree kernel on the same device; all-contribute needs `enabled()` isolation on CUDA-facade.
2. Whether `family` is part of v1 or the first PR hardcodes `"mm"` and adds the key later. This RFC keeps the key and only specifies `mm` configs.

issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Problem

Triton kernels in Inductor's orbit are usually tested the same way
everyone tests them: fixed power-of-two shapes, `torch.rand()`,
`allclose(rtol=1e-2)`. On a corpus of deliberately broken Triton
kernels I built, that standard test lets **88% of the planted bugs
pass** (14 of 16): tail tiles that never exist at benchmark shapes,
a `max` reduction seeded with `0.0` that non-negative inputs never
exercise, an fp16 accumulator that only stagnates above the tested
size, a row-stride mistake that is a no-op on contiguous tensors.
Two of the 16 bugs — an out-of-bounds write and a divergent
barrier — have no numerical signature at all, so no output
comparison at any shape or distribution can catch them.

## What I built

[litmus](https://github.com/NagaYu/litmus) (Apache-2.0) verifies
Triton kernels instead of sampling them, on CPU, with no GPU:

- **ToleranceBound** — a sound upper bound on the error a *correct*
  kernel may have (interval + affine arithmetic, an explicit
  reduction-order term, libm ULP budgets). The bound, not a guessed
  tolerance, becomes the threshold.
- **GPUSafetyCheck** — symbolic index analysis that proves
  in-bounds / race-freedom for all shapes first, and only searches
  for a concrete witness when a proof fails.
- **TargetedFalsification** — aimed input generators crossed with
  symbolic shape classes, plus SPSA ascent; counterexamples are
  delta-debugged to a median of 2 elements.

The verdict is three-valued — ACCEPT / REJECT / UNKNOWN — with CLI
exit codes 0 / 1 / 2, so CI decides what "unverified" means instead
of the tool folding it into "pass".

## Numbers (25-kernel corpus: 9 correct, 16 planted bugs)

| | standard allclose | strong fuzzing baseline | litmus |
|---|---|---|---|
| bug detection | 12% | 62% | **100%** |
| false positives | 0% | 0% | **0%** |
| wall clock (whole corpus, laptop, no GPU) | 0.5s | 1.0s | 40.9s |

- Live demo (runs entirely in the browser, nothing uploaded):
  https://huggingface.co/spaces/NagaYu/litmus
- Corpus with answer key:
  https://huggingface.co/datasets/NagaYu/litmus-kernels

## Proposal

I would like to offer this as a test-side utility for Inductor /
Triton kernel work — e.g. an optional stricter check for generated
kernels in CI, or a starting point for discussing what a sound
tolerance for kernel tests should look like. Happy to adapt the
shape of the integration (standalone tool, test helper, or a
reduced version of the bound checker) to what maintainers find
useful, and to send a PR if there is interest.

Portfolio: https://nagayu-portfolio.nagayu.workers.dev/en

### Alternatives
